title: The water cycle: where rain comes from and where it goes

summary.text: Every raindrop was once water on the land or in the sea. The Sun warms that water, and some of it evaporates into an invisible gas called water vapour. High up the air is cold, so the vapour condenses into tiny drops, and billions of drops make a cloud. The drops grow and fall as rain, hail or snow, and rivers carry the water back to the sea. Salt cannot evaporate, so rain is fresh even though most of it rose from the salty sea.
summary.art: A cut-away picture of India's west coast: the Arabian Sea with wavy lines rising from it, clouds drifting to the Western Ghats, rain falling on green hills, a river flowing back to the sea, and a big round arrow joining it all.

intro.hook: Wet your hand and press it flat on a dry floor tile in the sunshine. Watch your handprint. Count slowly. Where is the water going? It did not soak into the tile.
intro.text: In a minute or two, your handprint vanishes. The water has not been destroyed. It has gone into the air, as an invisible gas. It might come back down as rain next week, a hundred kilometres away. Every drop of rain you have ever seen went up first. This unit follows water on its round journey: up from the sea, into the clouds, down as rain, along rivers and back to the sea. You will make a real cloud in a jar, and get fresh water out of salty water using only sunshine.
intro.art: A wet child's handprint on a sunny floor tile, fading at the edges, with faint wavy lines rising from it towards a window full of sky.

outcomes: I can say what the water cycle is: water goes from the sea and the land up into the air, forms clouds, falls as rain, and flows back to the sea.
I can explain evaporation and condensation in plain words, and show both happening at home.
I can explain that clouds are made of tiny drops of water on specks of dust, and how those drops grow into rain, hail or snow.
I can explain why rain is fresh even though the sea is salty, and make fresh water from salty water with sunshine.
I can run a fair test of what makes water evaporate faster, and show the results in a table and a bar chart. I can show that plants put water into the air.
I can explain the monsoon as India's biggest water cycle, and why mountains make some places very wet and others dry.

I can explain that the Sun's energy drives the water cycle, and that the energy comes out again in storms. I can also say what scientists still do not know, and name a world with rain that is not water.

terms.meaning: The journey water makes again and again. It goes up from the sea and land into the air, comes down as rain or snow, and flows back to the sea. It has no start and no end.
terms.example: The rain on your roof today may have been in the Arabian Sea last week.
terms.art: A big circle of arrows joining the sea, a cloud, rain, a hill, a river and the sea again.

terms.meaning: One of the forms a material can take. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
terms.example: Water in a glass, milk in a cup and oil in a bottle are liquids.
terms.art: Water being poured from a lota into a steel tumbler.

terms.meaning: One of the forms a material can take. A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can. Most gases are invisible.
terms.example: The air around you is a mix of gases. You cannot see it, but you can feel it as wind.
terms.art: A balloon being blown up, with tiny dots spreading out inside it.

terms.meaning: Water as a gas. It is completely invisible. There is always some in the air around you.
terms.example: On a sticky monsoon day, the air is full of water vapour. That is why your clothes take so long to dry.
terms.art: A clear glass of air with tiny, far-apart water dots drawn inside, and a label saying 'invisible'.

terms.meaning: When liquid water slowly turns into water vapour and goes into the air. Heat, wind and sunshine make it faster.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because their water evaporates.
terms.art: Clothes on a terrace washing line in the sun, with faint wavy lines rising from them.

terms.meaning: When water vapour cools down and turns back into tiny drops of liquid water. It happens on cold surfaces, and in air that is cooling.
terms.example: Drops appear on the outside of a steel tumbler full of ice. They came out of the air.
terms.art: A cold steel tumbler with ice inside and shiny drops all over the outside.

terms.meaning: Steam is the water vapour that comes off boiling water. Like all water vapour, it is invisible. The white cloud you see above a kettle is tiny drops that have already condensed.
terms.example: Look closely at a boiling kettle's spout. Right next to it there is a clear gap. The white mist starts a little further away.
terms.art: A kettle spout with a clear gap, then a white curl of mist above it, with a small arrow pointing at the clear gap.

terms.meaning: A huge crowd of tiny water drops, or tiny ice crystals, floating in the air. Each drop is far too small to see by itself.
terms.example: A white cloud over the hills is made of billions and billions of tiny drops.
terms.art: A fluffy white cloud with a magnifying glass showing tiny round drops inside it.

terms.meaning: A tiny speck of dust, salt, smoke or pollen floating in the air. Water vapour condenses onto it to make a cloud drop. The plural is condensation nuclei.
terms.example: Over the sea, tiny grains of salt from sea spray become the seeds of cloud drops.
terms.art: A single tiny speck of dust in the air with a water drop growing around it.

terms.meaning: Drops of water that form on cool grass, leaves and cars on a still night. The water comes out of the air, by condensation.
terms.example: On a winter morning, the grass in the park is wet even though it did not rain.
terms.art: Shiny dew drops on blades of grass and a spider's web in early morning light.

terms.meaning: A cloud that sits on the ground. Mist is a thin one. Fog is a thick one you can hardly see through.
terms.example: In winter, Delhi and Punjab often have thick fog in the early morning, and trains run late.
terms.art: A road in the early morning with trees fading into white fog.

terms.meaning: Any water that falls from clouds to the ground: rain, drizzle, hail or snow. It is a long word for 'falling water'.
terms.example: Rain in Mumbai, hail in a summer storm in Bihar and snow in Kashmir are all precipitation.
terms.art: Three panels: rain, hailstones bouncing on a road, and snow on a pine tree.

terms.meaning: Balls of ice that fall from big storm clouds. They grow as they are tossed up and down inside the cloud.
terms.example: A hailstorm can dent car roofs and damage crops, even on a hot day.
terms.art: Small white hailstones bouncing on a tin roof.

terms.meaning: Plants giving off water vapour from tiny holes in their leaves. The water comes up from the roots, through the stem.
terms.example: A big tree can put many buckets of water into the air on one hot day.
terms.art: A neem tree with tiny wavy lines rising from its leaves and arrows showing water going up from the roots.

terms.meaning: The smallest piece of water that is still water. Each water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom. One drop has more molecules than there are grains of sand on all the beaches of India.
terms.example: When a puddle evaporates, its molecules fly off into the air one by one.
terms.art: A drop of water with a zoom-in circle showing tiny V-shaped molecules jostling.

terms.meaning: What it takes to make something move, warm up or change. Energy never disappears. It only changes from one kind into another.
terms.example: The Sun's heat gives water the energy to evaporate. That energy comes out again when the vapour turns back into drops.
terms.art: The Sun shining on the sea, with a glowing arrow going up into a cloud.

terms.meaning: A season of strong, wet winds that blow from the sea onto the land and bring heavy rain. In most of India, the monsoon comes from June to September.
terms.example: The monsoon usually reaches Kerala around the first of June. Farmers wait for it to sow their crops.
terms.art: Dark monsoon clouds rolling in over coconut palms on the Kerala coast.

terms.meaning: A dry area on the far side of mountains. The wet wind drops most of its rain on the near side, so little is left.
terms.example: Mumbai, on the sea side of the Western Ghats, gets about three times as much rain as Pune, on the far side.
terms.art: A mountain range with rain pouring on the left slope and a dry, sunny plain on the right.

terms.meaning: Humid air has a lot of water vapour in it. It feels sticky, and sweat does not dry easily.
terms.example: Chennai in summer is humid. A Rajasthan summer is dry.
terms.art: A sweaty child fanning themselves on a sticky day, with a towel that won't dry.

terms.meaning: A flat, shallow pond where sea water is left in the sun. The water evaporates and the salt is left behind for people to collect.
terms.example: Most of India's salt comes from salt pans in Gujarat.
terms.art: Shallow square ponds of sea water with white heaps of salt and workers with wooden rakes.

terms.meaning: A simple machine that uses sunshine to make fresh water from salty or dirty water. The water evaporates, condenses on a cover and drips into a cup.
terms.example: You will build one with a bowl, a cup and cling film.
terms.art: A bowl of salty water with a small cup in the middle, covered with cling film dipping down over a pebble, and drops running into the cup.

terms.meaning: A gas we use as fuel. On Earth it is a gas, but on Saturn's very cold moon Titan it is a liquid, and it falls as rain.
terms.example: The piped gas that some city kitchens cook with, and biogas made from cow dung, are mostly methane.
terms.art: A blue gas flame on a stove, next to an orange, hazy moon with dark lakes.

explanations.definition: The water cycle is the journey water makes round and round. It rises from the sea and the land into the air, forms clouds, falls as rain or snow, and flows back to the sea.
explanations.description: The water cycle has four big steps. First, the Sun warms water, and some of it rises into the air as an invisible gas. This is evaporation. Second, high up the air is cold, and the gas turns back into tiny drops that make clouds. This is condensation. Third, the drops grow and fall as rain, hail or snow. This is precipitation. Fourth, the water gathers in rivers, lakes, the ground and the sea. Then it starts again. The cycle has no beginning and no end. You can join it anywhere. Almost no water leaves the Earth, and almost no new water arrives. The same water just keeps going round.
examples: A puddle dries in the sun. Its water is now in the air, and will fall as rain somewhere.
The Ganga carries rain and melted snow from the Himalaya to the Bay of Bengal. From the sea, the water rises again.
Your breath on a cold mirror makes a tiny cloud, and it dries up again in seconds.
explanations.art: A simple circle picture: the sea with wavy arrows going up, a cloud, rain falling on hills, a river running down to the sea, each step labelled with its name.
explanations.context: Water in a puddle, a cloud and a river is the same water at different moments. This card names the four big steps of its round journey.

explanations.concept: Evaporation: water going into the air as a gas
explanations.definition: Evaporation is liquid water slowly turning into water vapour, an invisible gas, and mixing into the air. It happens at any temperature, not only when water boils.
explanations.description: Water is made of tiny particles called molecules. They are always jiggling and bumping into each other. At the top of a puddle, some molecules jiggle so fast that they break free and fly off into the air. That is evaporation. Warmth makes the molecules jiggle faster, so more of them escape. Wind blows the escaped molecules away, so they don't fall back in. A wide puddle has a bigger surface than a narrow glass, so more molecules can escape at once. Dry air takes up vapour more easily than sticky, humid air. So clothes dry fastest on a hot, windy, dry day, spread out flat.
examples: Wet clothes on a terrace dry faster in the sun and wind than in a closed bathroom.
A wide plate of water dries up long before the same water in a narrow glass.
In the Rajasthan summer, a wet floor dries in minutes. In a sticky Mumbai monsoon, it can take an hour.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in puddle surface with tiny molecules jiggling, and a few fast ones flying up and away, blown by a little breeze.
explanations.context: Wet clothes dry even when nothing heats them to boiling. This card explains how water slips into the air by itself, and what makes it faster.

explanations.concept: Water vapour is invisible, and so is real steam
explanations.definition: Water vapour is a gas, and it is completely invisible. The white mist above a kettle or a pressure cooker is not vapour. It is a crowd of tiny liquid drops that have already condensed.
explanations.description: The air in your room right now has water vapour in it. You cannot see it, smell it or feel it. Look closely at a kettle as it boils. Right at the spout there is a small clear gap. That gap is the real, invisible steam. A little further out, the steam meets cooler air and turns back into tiny drops. Those drops are what you see as white mist. So the white puff from a pressure cooker whistle is really a tiny cloud. Clouds in the sky are made the same way.
examples: The clear gap just above a kettle spout is the invisible steam.
On a cold morning in Shimla, you can 'see your breath'. You are seeing tiny drops, not vapour.
A drying shirt sends water into the air, but you never see it go.
explanations.art: A kettle spout with a clear gap labelled 'invisible steam', then a white curl labelled 'tiny drops: a little cloud'.
explanations.context: Many people think the white 'steam' over a kettle is water vapour. This card shows where the invisible vapour really is.

explanations.concept: Condensation: water coming back out of the air
explanations.definition: Condensation is water vapour cooling down and turning back into tiny drops of liquid water. It happens when vapour touches something cold, or when air cools as it rises.
explanations.description: Cold makes molecules slow down. When vapour molecules touch a cold surface, they slow down, stick to it and to each other, and make drops. That is condensation, and it is evaporation run backwards. So any cold surface collects water from the air. A steel tumbler of ice gets wet on the outside. The inside of a lid over hot rice drips. The grass gets dew on a cool night. Air that rises up a mountain or high into the sky also cools, and its vapour condenses into clouds.
examples: A cold steel tumbler gets wet on the outside on a sticky day. The drops came from the air, not through the steel.
The underside of the lid on a pot of hot dal is covered in drops.
Car windows mist up from the inside when a whole family breathes in a closed car.
explanations.art: A cold steel tumbler with ice inside, and arrows showing invisible vapour from the air sticking to the outside as shiny drops.
explanations.context: A tumbler of ice gets wet on the outside, though no water leaked through. This card explains where those drops come from.

explanations.concept: Clouds: tiny drops on specks of dust
explanations.definition: A cloud is a huge crowd of tiny water drops, or tiny ice crystals, floating in the air. Each drop forms around a speck of dust, salt, smoke or pollen.
explanations.description: Vapour finds it hard to make a drop out of nothing. It needs something to stick to. In the air there are billions of tiny specks: dust, salt from sea spray, smoke and pollen. Vapour condenses onto them, and each speck grows into a cloud drop. A Scottish scientist, John Aitken, showed this in 1880. He filtered all the dust out of air in a jar, and then it would not make a cloud. Cloud drops are tiny, about one hundredth of a millimetre across. They are so small and light that rising air holds them up, and they fall very slowly. But a whole cloud is heavy. An American cloud scientist, Peggy LeMone, worked out that one ordinary puffy cloud holds about 500,000 kilograms of water. That is as heavy as about 100 elephants, spread out over a huge space.
examples: Smoke from an agarbatti, an incense stick, helps the cloud in a jar form much faster.
Over the sea, tiny grains of salt from sea spray are the seeds of many cloud drops.
Clouds look white because their billions of drops scatter sunlight. Very thick clouds look grey or dark because less light gets through.
explanations.art: A puffy white cloud with a zoom-in circle showing tiny drops, each with a dark speck of dust or salt in its middle.
explanations.context: Clouds look soft and weightless. This card explains what they are really made of, and how heavy they are.

explanations.description: A raindrop is about 100 times wider than a cloud drop. So it takes about a million cloud drops to make one raindrop. Scientists know two ways this happens. But in warm clouds over India, rain often forms faster than these ideas can fully explain. How exactly it happens so fast is still being studied.
examples: Rain can pour out of a big monsoon cloud within half an hour of it forming.
In cold clouds, high up, rain often starts as snow and melts on the way down.
One raindrop holds about as much water as a million cloud drops.

perspectives.who: Alfred Wegener (1911), Tor Bergeron (1933) and Walter Findeisen (1938), German and Swedish weather scientists
perspectives.explanation: In the cold top of a cloud, ice crystals and supercooled drops sit side by side. Supercooled drops are drops colder than freezing that have not frozen yet. The ice crystals grow by taking water from the drops. They become heavy snowflakes, fall, and melt into rain on the way down.

perspectives.who: Many weather scientists, for warm tropical clouds
perspectives.explanation: In warm clouds there is no ice. Bigger drops fall a little faster, bump into smaller ones and swallow them. This is called collision and coalescence. It works best when the cloud has a few big seeds, like grains of sea salt.

perspectives.who: Scientists studying clouds today, including in India
perspectives.explanation: Swirling, bumpy air inside clouds, called turbulence, may throw drops together much more often. That could explain why rain forms so fast. Exactly how much turbulence matters is still argued about. Computers and cloud experiments are testing it.

explanations.art: A cloud cut open: tiny drops bumping and joining into bigger drops at the bottom, and ice crystals growing at the cold top.
explanations.context: A cloud drop is far too small and light to fall as rain. This card is about how a million of them become one raindrop, which scientists are still working out.

explanations.definition: Precipitation is any water falling from clouds: rain, drizzle, hail or snow. Which one falls depends on how cold the cloud and the air below it are.
explanations.description: Drizzle is very small drops from low, thin clouds. Rain is bigger drops. Snow is ice crystals that stay frozen all the way down, as in Kashmir and Ladakh in winter. Hail is balls of ice from huge storm clouds. Strong rising winds keep them up inside the cloud, where they collect layer after layer of ice, like an onion. Raindrops are not shaped like teardrops. Small ones are round. Bigger ones are squashed flat at the bottom, like a burger bun, by the air they fall through. Very big drops wobble and break apart before they reach the ground.
examples: A cut-open hailstone shows rings, like an onion. Each ring is a layer of ice it collected while the winds kept it up in the cloud.
Snow falls in Gulmarg in winter. The same kind of cloud over Delhi would give rain, because the warmer air near the ground melts the snow on the way down.
Drawings of raindrops as teardrops are wrong. Real falling drops look like little buns.
explanations.art: Four panels: fine drizzle, round and bun-shaped raindrops, a hailstone cut open showing rings, and a six-sided snowflake.
explanations.context: Rain, drizzle, hail and snow all fall from clouds. This card explains what makes them different, and the real shape of a raindrop.

explanations.concept: Why rain is fresh but the sea is salty
explanations.definition: When sea water evaporates, only the water goes up into the air. The salt stays behind. So rain is fresh water, even though most of it rose from the salty sea.
explanations.description: Salt is dissolved in the sea, about 6 teaspoons in every litre. When the Sun warms the sea, water molecules break free and fly up. Salt cannot evaporate at these temperatures, so it is left behind. This is why salt pans work: people let sea water evaporate in the sun and rake up the salt. Rivers carry tiny amounts of salt from rocks into the sea. The water leaves again as vapour, but the salt cannot. Over hundreds of millions of years, this has made the sea salty. A solar still copies the sky. It lets salty water evaporate, catches the vapour on a cover, and collects fresh drops.
examples: Gujarat's salt pans make most of India's salt, just by letting sea water evaporate.
Rain water caught in a clean bowl is not salty, even at the seaside.
A salty tear or sweat dries to leave a white mark on your skin or shirt. The water left, the salt stayed.
explanations.art: A cut-away of the sea with water molecules rising as vapour into a cloud, while little salt cubes stay behind in the water.
explanations.context: Most rain rises from the salty sea, yet rain is not salty. This card explains why, and how salt pans and solar stills use the same trick.

explanations.concept: Plants put water into the air
explanations.definition: Transpiration is plants giving off water vapour through tiny holes in their leaves. The water is pulled up from the roots, through the stem, to the leaves.
explanations.description: A plant drinks through its roots. Most of that water does not stay in the plant. It travels up the stem and leaves through tiny holes, too small to see, on the underside of leaves. As this water evaporates, it pulls more water up behind it, like sipping through a straw. A big tree can give off more than a hundred litres on a hot day. So a forest puts a huge amount of invisible water vapour into the air. Some of the rain that falls far inland, in Central India or the Amazon rainforest, has already been through the leaves of trees on the way. Scientists think more than half of the water rising from land comes out through plants. Exactly how much is still argued about.
examples: A clear bag tied over a leafy branch in the sun turns misty inside within an hour.
The shade of a tree feels cooler than the shade of a wall, partly because its leaves give off water, and evaporation takes heat away.
In the Amazon, water goes from rain to tree to cloud to rain again, many times, as the winds carry it inland.
explanations.art: A leafy tree with blue arrows going up the trunk from the roots and faint wavy lines rising from the leaves into a cloud above.
explanations.context: Plants are part of the water cycle too. This card is about how leaves put water into the air.

explanations.concept: The Sun's energy drives the water cycle
explanations.definition: The Sun's energy drives the water cycle. Water needs energy to evaporate. When the vapour condenses into cloud drops, that energy comes out again as heat.
explanations.description: To break free and fly off, water molecules need energy, and they take it from the Sun's warmth. That is why wet skin feels cold: evaporation takes heat away. The energy is not lost. It travels up inside the vapour. When the vapour condenses in a cloud, the energy comes out again, and warms the air around it. Warm air rises, so the cloud grows taller. This is how a small cloud can grow into a huge thundercloud in an afternoon. Cyclones over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea get their great strength this way, from warm sea water that evaporates and condenses. Gravity does the other half of the work. It pulls rain down and makes rivers flow to the sea.
examples: Wet hands feel cold in a breeze, because evaporation takes heat away.
A tall thundercloud on a summer afternoon is powered by energy from vapour turning into drops.
Cyclones form only over warm seas, and they get weaker once they move over land.
explanations.art: The Sun shining on the sea, glowing arrows rising inside vapour, and a tall thundercloud where the glow comes out as heat, with a lightning flash.
explanations.context: Something has to lift all that water into the sky. This card explains where the energy comes from, and where it goes.

explanations.concept: The monsoon: India's giant water cycle
explanations.definition: The monsoon is a season of wet winds that blow from the sea onto the land and bring heavy rain. In most of India, it comes from June to September and gives most of the year's rain.
explanations.description: In early summer, the land of India gets very hot. Wind starts blowing in from the cooler Indian Ocean and Arabian Sea, carrying huge amounts of water vapour. When this wet air meets mountains, like the Western Ghats or the hills of the North-East, it is pushed upwards. Rising air cools, the vapour condenses, and rain pours down on the sea side of the mountains. Little is left for the far side, which stays drier. That dry side is called a rain shadow. The monsoon usually reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers all of India by about 8 July. Mawsynram and Sohra, also called Cherrapunji, in Meghalaya, get more than 11 metres of rain in a year. They are among the wettest places on Earth.
examples: Mumbai, on the sea side of the Western Ghats, gets about three times as much rain as Pune, on the far side.
Farmers across India wait for the monsoon before sowing rice, cotton and many other crops.
The rivers of the Western Ghats, like the Kaveri, swell after the monsoon reaches the hills.
explanations.art: A map of India with arrows of wet wind blowing in from the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal, rain clouds piled against the Western Ghats and the Meghalaya hills, and a dry rain shadow beyond.
explanations.context: Most of India's water arrives in about four months of the year. This card explains the monsoon as the water cycle at its biggest.

explanations.description: Everyone agrees on what the monsoon does. Why it happens is a harder question. Scientists have given different answers, and they still argue about how much each one matters.
examples: Small sea breezes blow onto the land on hot afternoons at Chennai or Mumbai beaches. Is the monsoon a giant version?
The Tibetan plateau, a huge high land north of the Himalaya, gets very hot in summer.

perspectives.who: Edmond Halley, an English scientist, in 1686, and many school books
perspectives.explanation: The monsoon is a giant sea breeze. In summer, the land heats up faster than the sea. Hot air over the land rises, and cooler, wet air from the sea flows in to take its place.

The sea breeze idea is only part of it. Around the Earth's middle there is a belt of rising air and rain. In summer, this rain belt moves north, over India, following the Sun. The monsoon is that rain belt arriving.
The high, hot Tibetan plateau and the Himalaya act like a giant heater and a wall. They help pull the monsoon in and keep it there. How much this matters compared with the rain belt is still debated.

explanations.art: A globe showing a band of rain clouds sliding north over India in summer, with the hot Tibetan plateau glowing behind the Himalaya.
explanations.context: Why does the wind turn wet and blow onto India every June? This card is about the different answers scientists have given.

explanations.concept: How long water stays in each place
explanations.definition: Water stays in different parts of the cycle for very different times. On average, a drop stays in the air for only about 9 days, but it can stay in the sea for thousands of years.
explanations.description: The water cycle has fast parts and slow parts. Water in the air comes down again in about 9 days on average. Water in a river reaches the sea in a few weeks or months. In the deep sea, a drop may stay for about 3,000 years before it evaporates again. Deep groundwater can wait thousands of years. The ice deep in Antarctica is the slowest of all. Scientists have drilled out Antarctic ice that froze about 800,000 years ago, and found tiny bubbles of ancient air inside it.
examples: Rain from a monsoon cloud today was probably sea water less than two weeks ago.
A drop that sinks into the deep sea may not rise again for 3,000 years.
Some ice in Antarctica froze long before the first modern humans, about 300,000 years ago.
explanations.art: A time strip: a cloud labelled '9 days', a river labelled 'weeks', the sea labelled '3,000 years', and a block of Antarctic ice labelled '800,000 years'.
explanations.context: Some water whizzes round the cycle and some waits for ages. This card shows how long a drop usually stays in each place.

explanations.concept: People are part of the water cycle now
explanations.definition: People now change the water cycle a lot. Dams, canals, borewells and cities move huge amounts of water, and a warmer world puts more water vapour into the air.
explanations.description: Most water cycle pictures show only sea, clouds, mountains and rivers. In 2019, a team of scientists led by Benjamin Abbott looked at hundreds of these pictures. Most of them left people out completely. But people store rivers behind dams, pump up groundwater for farms, and cover land with cement so rain runs off. A warmer world matters too. Warmer air can hold more water vapour, about 7 more parts in every 100 for each degree of warming. So when it rains, it can pour harder. In 2017, Roxy Mathew Koll and others found that days of very heavy rain over central India had become about three times more common since 1950.
examples: A dam on a river holds back water that would have flowed to the sea.
Water pumped from a borewell to a rice field evaporates or soaks in, instead of staying underground.
Some cities flood in the monsoon and run short of water in summer.
explanations.art: A water cycle picture that includes a dam, a borewell, a farm with sprinklers and a city of cement, with the arrows passing through them.
explanations.context: Most water cycle pictures leave people out. This card shows how people now change the water cycle.

explanations.description: Some tiny living things, too small to see, are carried high into the clouds by the wind. Some kinds of bacteria are very good at helping water freeze. In 2008, Brent Christner and other scientists tested fresh snow from several countries. Many of the specks that started its ice crystals came from living things, including bacteria. These specks help ice crystals start forming in clouds at temperatures where water would usually stay liquid. Some scientists think this could help the bacteria. They ride up from leaves, help make rain or snow, and fall back down onto new plants. This idea is called bioprecipitation. Scientists are still finding out how much it really matters for the world's rain.
examples: A single type of bacteria that lives on leaves is one of the best ice-makers known.
Fresh snow collected in several different countries had these ice-making specks from living things in it.
explanations.art: A cloud with a zoom-in showing a tiny rod-shaped bacterium inside a growing ice crystal, and leaves far below.
explanations.context: Clouds are not only water and dust. This card is about tiny living things that may help make rain and snow.

explanations.definition: Other worlds have their own weather cycles. On Titan, Saturn's biggest moon, it rains liquid methane, which fills rivers and lakes.
explanations.description: Titan is so cold, about 180 degrees below zero, that water is rock-hard ice there. But methane, which is a gas on Earth, is a liquid on Titan. It evaporates from lakes, makes clouds, and falls as slow, heavy rain. It carves rivers and fills seas. In January 2005, a probe called Huygens landed on Titan and photographed river channels and pebbles. Another spacecraft, Cassini, flew past Titan many times and found big lakes and seas near its poles. Venus has clouds of sulphuric acid, a strong acid. Acid drops fall from them, but the air below is so hot that they evaporate long before they reach the ground. So a cycle of evaporation, clouds and rain can happen with other liquids too.
examples: Titan is the only place we know, other than Earth, with rain, rivers and lakes on its surface today.
On Venus, acid drops fall from the clouds but evaporate high above the ground.
explanations.art: Titan's orange, hazy sky with a dark methane lake, pebbles on the shore, and slow fat drops falling.
explanations.context: Earth is not the only world with rain. This card visits a moon where the rain is not water.

explanations.concept: How people found out that rain feeds rivers
explanations.definition: We know that rivers and springs are fed by rain and melting snow, because people measured the rain and the rivers and found the rain was more than enough.
explanations.description: For about two thousand years, many learned people thought rain was far too little to keep rivers flowing all year. They believed rivers were fed by sea water rising through secret passages under the mountains. In 1580, Bernard Palissy, a French potter who never went to university, wrote that rivers and springs come only from rain soaking into the ground. Scholars took little notice of him. About ninety years later, Pierre Perrault measured the rain falling on the land around the start of the river Seine for three years. In 1674, he showed it was about six times more than the river carried. Edmond Halley then measured how fast water evaporates from a pan. He showed that the Sun lifts enough water from the sea to make all the rain.
examples: Palissy was right, but he had no measurements, so few people believed him.
You can do Perrault's kind of work at home: measure the rain with a bottle, and the evaporation with a plate.
explanations.art: A 17th-century man in a long coat reading a rain gauge beside a river, with a notebook of numbers.
explanations.context: Today everyone learns that rain feeds rivers. This card tells how people found that out, and who said it first.

agreed.text: Water goes round and round between the sea, the air and the land. Very little water leaves the Earth or arrives from space.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measure rain, river flow and evaporation all over the world. Year after year, the water that goes up and the water that comes down roughly balance.

agreed.text: Clouds are made of tiny liquid drops or ice crystals, not of water vapour.
agreed.evidence: Aeroplanes fitted with instruments fly through clouds and collect the drops. Vapour is invisible, but clouds can be seen, because their drops scatter light.

agreed.text: When sea water evaporates, the salt stays behind. So rain is fresh water.
agreed.evidence: Salt pans have made salt this way for thousands of years. Rain water tested near the sea has almost no salt in it.

agreed.text: The Sun's energy drives evaporation, and that energy comes out again when vapour condenses into clouds.
agreed.evidence: Wet skin cools as water evaporates. Weather balloons show that air rising inside a cloud cools more slowly than dry rising air, because condensing vapour gives out heat.

agreed.text: Rivers and springs are fed by rain and melting snow.
agreed.evidence: In 1674, Pierre Perrault showed that the rain around the river Seine was about six times more than the river carried. River levels across India rise after the monsoon rain.

agreed.text: Warmer air can hold more water vapour, so a warmer world gets heavier downpours.
agreed.evidence: This follows from basic physics, and weather records show it. Studies of India's rain since 1950 find more days of very heavy rain over central India.

challenging.claim: Clouds are made of water vapour, or steam.
challenging.for: Clouds are made of water, and they float like a gas.
challenging.against: Water vapour is invisible. Clouds can be seen because they are made of tiny liquid drops or ice. The white mist above a kettle is tiny drops too, not vapour.

challenging.claim: Water only evaporates when it boils.
challenging.for: Boiling water clearly turns into steam, and we use heat to dry things fast.
challenging.against: A puddle dries on a cool day, and wet clothes dry in the shade. Water evaporates at any temperature. Heat only makes it faster.

challenging.claim: Rivers and springs are fed by sea water rising through passages under the mountains.
challenging.who: Many learned people in Europe for about two thousand years, until the 1600s
challenging.for: Rivers flow all year, even in dry months. People could not believe rain was enough.
challenging.against: Bernard Palissy argued against it in 1580. Pierre Perrault measured it in 1674, and found the rain was about six times what the river carried. Springs are fresh, not salty, too.

challenging.claim: The water cycle is a neat circle of sea, clouds, rain and rivers, untouched by people.
challenging.who: Most water cycle pictures in books and on websites
challenging.for: It is a simple way to show the main journey.
challenging.against: In 2019, scientists led by Benjamin Abbott checked hundreds of these pictures, and most left people out. Today, dams, borewells, farms and cities move huge amounts of water.

challenging.claim: Cloud seeding can make it rain whenever we want.
challenging.who: Some news reports, and some companies that sell it
challenging.for: Since 1946, when Vincent Schaefer made snow in a cold box with dry ice, seeding clouds with tiny specks has made some clouds rain or snow more.
challenging.against: Seeding only works on the right kind of cloud, which must already be close to raining. Scientists at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology in Pune tested it over Solapur in Maharashtra. They found it can add some rain, but only from suitable clouds. It cannot make rain from a clear sky.

challenging.claim: Forests draw wet air in from the sea, like a pump.
challenging.who: Anastassia Makarieva and Victor Gorshkov, two Russian scientists, in 2007. They call it the 'biotic pump'.
challenging.for: Forests give off huge amounts of water vapour. When it condenses, the air pressure drops, and that could draw wet air in from the sea. Inland forests like the Amazon really do recycle rain many times.
challenging.against: Many weather scientists agree that forests recycle rain. But they doubt that forests pull in sea air as strongly as the biotic pump says. The argument is still going on.

challenging.for: Drops dripping off a tap look like teardrops, so it seems natural.
challenging.against: High-speed photos show falling raindrops are round when small and flattened like a bun when bigger. The teardrop shape only appears as a drop clings to a tap, just before it falls.

big_questions.q: Is a cloud a thing, or is it something that keeps happening?
big_questions.hint: A cloud's drops keep forming at the bottom and drying up at the edges. Is it the same cloud a minute later?

big_questions.q: Why is rain fresh when most of it rose from the salty sea?
big_questions.hint: Think about the salt pans. What goes up, and what stays behind?

big_questions.q: When a puddle dries, it takes heat from the ground. Where does that heat go?
big_questions.hint: It rides up inside the vapour. What happens when the vapour turns back into drops in a cloud?

big_questions.q: A forest in one country helps make rain that falls in another. If someone cuts down that forest, have they taken someone else's rain?
big_questions.hint: Who should decide what happens to a forest?

big_questions.q: One country seeds a cloud and it rains there. Maybe that cloud would have rained on the next country. Is that fair?
big_questions.hint: Who owns a cloud as it drifts across a border?

big_questions.q: You breathe out water and sweat water every day, and you drink new water. Are you the same you as last year?
big_questions.hint: A river keeps its name while all its water changes. Is that like you?

big_questions.q: The same monsoon brings joy to a farmer and floods to a city. Can one thing be both good and bad?
big_questions.hint: What makes the difference: the rain, or what we have built?

big_questions.q: On Titan, it rains methane. Would you still call it rain?
big_questions.hint: What makes rain 'rain': what it is made of, or what it does?

big_questions.q: If the Sun stopped shining, what would happen to the water cycle?
big_questions.hint: Which steps need the Sun's energy? Which need gravity?

big_questions.q: For hundreds of years, poets in India have written about clouds and the monsoon. Kalidasa, a great poet, imagined a cloud carrying a message across India. Why do clouds make people feel so much?
big_questions.hint: How do you feel when the first monsoon clouds come? Why?

big_questions.q: Most water cycle pictures leave people out. Why do you think we draw nature without ourselves in it?
big_questions.hint: Draw your own water cycle. Where would your home go?

story.title: The Sky Under the Lid
story.note: Real: wooden dhows from Mandvi in Kutch did sail to Arabia and East Africa, using the monsoon winds, and there are salt pans along the Kutch coast. Ships really did make fresh water from sea water by boiling it and catching the steam. Amina, her father, the dhow Noor, the cook Yusuf and this voyage are made up.
text: Amina was ten, and she had never seen so much water and so little to drink.

The dhow was called Noor. She was a wooden ship from Mandvi, on the coast of Kutch, with one huge sail shaped like a slice of melon. Amina's father was her captain. They were sailing to Muscat, across the Arabian Sea, with a load of rice and cotton cloth. It was Amina's first voyage, and for six days the wind had pushed them along as if it were in a hurry too.
On the seventh day, the wind stopped.
It did not slow down. It simply stopped, the way a song stops. The great sail hung down like a tired elephant's ear. The sea went flat and shiny, as smooth as a steel plate, and it stayed that way.
On the ninth day, the sailors found that the biggest water barrel had cracked. Most of their drinking water had leaked into the bottom of the ship and mixed with the sea.
'How much is left?' asked her father.
Yusuf the cook tipped the last good barrel and listened to the slosh. 'Three days,' he said. 'Four, if nobody washes and nobody cries.'

Amina did not cry. But she was very thirsty, and all around her, as far as she could see, there was water. Blue water, green water, water so bright in the sun it hurt to look at. She leaned over the side and dipped her hand in. She licked one finger. It was so salty it stung.
'Don't,' said old Haroon, who had sailed for forty years. 'Drink the sea and the sea will drink you.' He told her about sailors who had gone mad with thirst and jumped in. Amina wished he had not.

That night, Yusuf cooked rice. He had no fresh water to spare for cooking, so he boiled the rice in sea water, in his big copper pot. He covered the pot with a heavy brass plate to keep the heat in. Amina sat beside him, hugging her knees, watching the little fire in its box of sand.
When the rice was done, Yusuf lifted the plate. Its underside was covered in shining drops. A few of them ran together and fell, plop, onto Amina's wrist.
Without thinking, she licked it.
Then she sat very still.
She licked her wrist again. She looked at the drops on the plate. She took one on her fingertip and put it on her tongue.
It was not salty. It tasted of nothing at all. It tasted of water.
'Yusuf,' she said. 'You cooked the rice in sea water.'
'I know I did. It will be salty. Eat it anyway.'
'But the drops on the lid aren't salty.'
Yusuf laughed, tiredly. 'Don't play games, little one.' But he touched a drop and tasted it. He stopped laughing.

Amina was thinking of home. Near Mandvi there were salt pans, long flat ponds where the salt workers let the sea in and closed it off. Then they waited. Day after day, the sun stood over the ponds, and the water went. Nobody carried it away. It went up, into the air, and left only salt behind, white and crunchy, in heaps taller than her father. Her mother used to say the sun was the thirstiest thing in the world. It drank the sea, but it would not drink the salt.
So where did the sun's drink go? Up. Into the air. And when it touched something cold, like this brass plate, it came back as water. Fresh water. The salt had stayed behind in the pot.
'The fire drinks the water out of the sea,' Amina said slowly, 'and the lid gives it back. Without the salt.'
Her father came over. Haroon came over. Everyone came over.

They worked all night. Yusuf filled the copper pot with sea water and kept the fire low and steady. Her father tilted the brass plate over it, so that the drops ran to one edge. Amina held a small cup under that edge. Haroon kept a wet cloth on top of the plate, dipping it again and again in the sea, because Amina said a cold lid would catch more. She did not know why. She only remembered that the cold steel tumblers at home grew drops on hot afternoons, and warm ones did not.

The drops came slowly. Plop. Plop. Plop. It took most of an hour to fill one small cup. They used up nearly a whole sack of firewood that night, and the cups they filled were not much. But each cup was a cup more than the sea would have given them.
For three days they boiled the sea. The sailors took turns at the fire. Nobody went mad. Nobody jumped in. The last barrel lasted, with the cups added, a little longer than Yusuf had said.

On the third evening, Amina was holding the cup when Haroon touched her shoulder and pointed. Far away, low over the flat sea, the sky had changed. Clouds were building up out of nothing. They rose and rose into towers, gold at the top from the setting sun, dark grey at the bottom.
Amina looked at the clouds, and then at the brass plate dripping into her cup.
'It's the same,' she whispered. 'The sun is heating the whole sea. And up there is the cold lid.'

That night the wind came back, and with it came the rain. Real rain, fat and cold, drumming on the deck and filling every bowl, every bucket and every empty barrel. The sailors danced in it with their mouths open. Amina stood at the rail and let it run down her face. It was not salty. It tasted of nothing at all. It tasted of water.

She thought of the salt pans at home, and the white heaps of salt, and the water that had risen out of them every day of her life. She had always thought it was simply gone. Now she knew where it went. It went up, and became this.
Somewhere under these same clouds, she thought, was Mandvi. Maybe it was raining there too, on her mother's roof, with water that had been this very sea a few days ago.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the key to the story is that when sea water evaporates, only the water goes up. The salt stays behind. Amina knows this from the salt pans, and she sees it again in the fresh drops on the lid of the rice pot. A cold surface turns the vapour back into drops. That is condensation. Her pot and plate are a small copy of the whole water cycle: the Sun heats the sea, the vapour rises, it condenses in the cold sky, and fresh rain falls. The story also quietly asks who is listened to: a ten-year-old girl noticed what the grown sailors had missed.
ask: Yusuf cooked the rice in sea water. Why were the drops on the brass plate not salty?
What did the salt pans at home help Amina understand?
Why did Amina want a wet cloth on top of the plate?
At the end, Amina says the clouds and the plate are 'the same'. What did she mean?
The sailors listened to a ten-year-old girl. Has anyone ever listened to an idea of yours? What happened?

games.title: Round the World Drop: the bead bracelet game
games.context: This is a game about the water cycle. You are a drop of water, travelling between 8 places in the room. You collect one coloured bead at each place, so your bracelet shows your journey.

printables.title: 8 place cards, one for each corner or table of the room
items: SEA (blue bead). Roll: 1, 2, 3: you stay deep in the sea. 4, 5: the Sun warms you, go to CLOUD. 6: a fish swallows you, go to ANIMAL.
CLOUD (white bead). Roll: 1: you drift on, stay. 2, 3, 4: you fall as rain into the SEA. 5: you fall on the hills, go to RIVER. 6: you fall as snow, go to ICE.
RIVER (green bead). Roll: 1, 2: you flow on, go to SEA. 3: you soak in, go to GROUND. 4: a cow drinks you, go to ANIMAL. 5: the Sun warms you, go to CLOUD. 6: a farmer's pump lifts you, go to PLANT.
GROUND (brown bead). Roll: 1, 2, 3: you wait between the grains, stay. 4: a root drinks you, go to PLANT. 5: you seep out as a spring, go to RIVER. 6: a well brings you up, go to ANIMAL.
PLANT (light green bead). Roll: 1: a cold night, you become a dewdrop on the leaf, go to DEW. 2, 3, 4, 5: you leave a leaf as vapour, go to CLOUD. 6: a goat eats the leaf, go to ANIMAL.
ANIMAL (red bead). Roll: 1, 2: you are breathed out, go to CLOUD. 3, 4: you leave as urine, go to GROUND. 5: you are sweat that dries, go to CLOUD. 6: you stay in the animal's body for now.
ICE (purple bead). Roll: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: you stay frozen in a glacier. 6: spring comes and you melt, go to RIVER.
DEW (yellow bead). Roll: 1, 2, 3: the morning Sun dries you, go to CLOUD. 4, 5, 6: you drip into the soil, go to GROUND.

printables.title: Beads or paper circles in 8 colours, and a piece of string or thread for each player
items: blue
white
green
brown
light green
red
purple
yellow

printables.title: My drop's journey
items: Turn number
Where I was
What I rolled
Where I went
The name of the change (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, soaking in, transpiration, melting)

rules: Put the 8 place cards in different spots around the room, with their beads beside them.
Everyone starts at the SEA, because most of Earth's water is in the sea. Take a blue bead and thread it.
On your turn, roll a dice and read your place card. Go where it tells you.
When you arrive, take that place's bead and thread it on your string. If you stay, take another bead of the same colour.
Say out loud the name of the change. For example, going from the sea to a cloud is evaporation.
Play 10 turns each. Then compare bracelets. Who visited the most different places? Did anyone get stuck in the ice?
Playing alone: play 10 turns, then play again with a second string. Are your two bracelets the same? Try to beat your own record for different places.

flow.do: 1. Print and cut out the 8 place cards. 2. Put each card in a different spot: a corner, a table, a chair, a doorway. 3. Put a pile of beads or coloured paper circles of the right colour beside each card. 4. Give each player a string with a knot at one end.
flow.say: You are each a tiny drop of water. Each of these places is part of the water cycle. You will travel around and collect a bead at each place you visit. Your bracelet will tell the story of your journey.
flow.kid: You are a drop of water! Put the 8 cards round the room. Put beads by each card. Tie a knot in your string.
flow.context: This is the first step of Round the World Drop. You set up 8 places from the water cycle around the room.

flow.do: Everyone starts at the SEA with a blue bead. Do the first roll together as practice.
flow.say: Most of Earth's water is in the sea, so that's where we start. Roll the dice and read the SEA card. Where do you go?
flow.kid: Start at the SEA. Take a blue bead. Roll the dice. Read the card. Where do you go?

check.q: In the game, you go from the SEA to a CLOUD. What is that change called?
options: Evaporation
Rain
Melting
check.why: Water leaves the sea as invisible vapour when the Sun warms it. That is evaporation. Later, the vapour cools and turns into the drops of a cloud.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll and move. 2. At each place, the player threads a bead and says the name of the change. 3. Fill in the score sheet together.
flow.say: Remember to say the name of the change as you move. Cloud to sea is precipitation, falling as rain. Plant to cloud is transpiration.
flow.kid: Roll and move. Thread a bead. Say the name of the change. Write it on your sheet.

ask.q: Why do you think the ICE card makes you stay so often?
good: Ice in a glacier stays frozen for a very long time.
It only melts when spring comes.

ask.q: Why does the SEA card make you stay so often?
good: The sea is huge and deep.
Water stays in the sea for thousands of years.

flow.parent: The dice chances are a rough copy of the real world. Water stays in the sea and in ice for a long time, so those cards often say 'stay'. A cloud lets water go fast, because water stays in the air only about 9 days. Rain mostly falls back into the sea, because the sea covers most of the Earth.

flow.do: After 10 turns each, lay the bracelets side by side and compare.
flow.say: Look at all our bracelets. Is any journey the same as another? Which colour do you have most of?
flow.kid: Look at your bracelet. Which colour do you have most of? Is anyone's bracelet the same as yours?

check.q: In the game, nobody's bracelet was quite the same. What does that show about the real water cycle?
options: Every drop takes its own path, but they all keep going round
Water always goes sea, cloud, river, sea in the same order
Some water stops for ever
check.why: Real drops do not follow one neat circle. A drop may go sea, cloud, sea, or river, ground, plant, cloud. But they all keep moving round. Picking 'the same order' usually comes from the neat circle drawn in books.

flow.do: Let each player wear their bracelet and tell their drop's story in three sentences.
flow.say: Tell me your drop's story, using your beads. Start with 'I began in the sea.'
flow.kid: Wear your bracelet. Tell your drop's story. Start with: I began in the sea.
flow.think: The water in your glass today has its own long bracelet of places. What might be on it?

games.title: Sun, Cold, Heavy! The molecule game
games.context: This is a running and acting game. Everyone is a water molecule, the smallest piece of water. A caller shouts 'Sun!', 'Cold!' or 'Heavy!', and the molecules show what water does.

printables.title: 12 caller cards to shuffle
items: SUN! Molecules jiggle fast and spread out all over the room. You are vapour.
COLD! Slow down. Hold hands with one or two others. You are a cloud drop.
HEAVY! Join into a group of four or more, crouch down and 'fall' to the floor. You are rain.
FREEZE! Stand still, holding hands in a pattern. You are ice.
MELT! Let go and wobble slowly around. You are liquid water again.
WIND! Everyone who is vapour drifts to one side of the room.
MOUNTAIN! Vapour molecules must climb onto the 'mountain' cushion and get COLD there.
LEAF! Two molecules crawl up the 'tree' chair and fly off as vapour.
SUN on the SEA! Only molecules in the 'sea' corner can jiggle and spread out.
COLD TUMBLER! Vapour molecules who touch the steel tumbler on the table stick together as dew.
SPECK! The caller drops a rolled-up sock on the floor. Molecules must gather round it to make a drop.
SALT! One player is salt. When SUN is called, salt cannot fly. It stays in the sea.

printables.title: Signs for the room
items: SEA (a corner)
MOUNTAIN (a cushion or a low stool)
TREE (a chair)
COLD TUMBLER (a steel tumbler on a table)

rules: One person is the caller. Everyone else is a water molecule. With only one child, the parent calls and the child plays, then swap.
Everyone starts in the SEA corner, wobbling slowly. That is liquid water.
The caller shuffles the cards, turns one over and shouts what it says.
The molecules must do it as fast as they can. The last one to do it right becomes the next caller.
After 12 cards, everyone says one change they acted out, and its name.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space. 2. Put up the four signs. SEA goes in a corner, MOUNTAIN on a cushion, TREE on a chair, and COLD TUMBLER on a table. 3. Shuffle the caller cards.
flow.say: Water is made of tiny particles called molecules. They are always moving. In this game, you are a molecule. Listen for my call, and do what water would do.
flow.kid: You are a water molecule, the smallest piece of water. Start in the SEA corner. Wobble slowly. Listen for the call!
flow.context: This is the first step of Sun, Cold, Heavy! Everyone acts as a water molecule, and a caller shouts what happens to the water.

flow.do: 1. Turn over a card and shout it. 2. Watch who does it right. 3. The last one becomes the next caller. 4. Play all 12 cards.
flow.say: SUN! Jiggle fast and spread out! You've evaporated. You're vapour now, invisible gas, all over the room.
flow.kid: Listen! Do the call as fast as you can. Sun means spread out. Cold means hold hands. Heavy means fall!
flow.parent: Keep the running gentle on a smooth floor. The big ideas to look for: heat spreads molecules apart into a gas. Cold brings them together into drops. Drops join until they are heavy enough to fall. Salt never flies with the vapour. The SPECK card shows that cloud drops need a speck to form on.

check.q: In the game, the call was 'COLD!' and molecules held hands. What real change was that?
options: Condensation: vapour turning back into drops
Evaporation: water going into the air
Boiling
check.why: Cold slows molecules down, so they stick together and make drops. That is condensation. Evaporation is the opposite, when molecules spread out and fly off. In the game, holding hands means you are a drop.

flow.do: Sit down together. Each player names one change they acted out, and says its name.
flow.say: Which change did you like acting most? What is its real name?
flow.kid: Sit down. Which call did you like best? What is its real name?
flow.think: When the SALT player could not fly with the vapour, what did that show about rain?
