items.p: What is the water cycle?
opts: The journey water makes round and round between the sea, the air and the land
A bicycle that runs on water
items.why: The water cycle is water's round journey: up into the air, down as rain or snow, and back to the sea. Picking 'rain falling once' sees only one step of the journey.

items.p: When water slowly turns into an invisible gas and goes into the air, we say it ____.
items.why: Evaporation is liquid water turning into water vapour. It happens to puddles, wet clothes and the sea.

items.p: When water vapour cools and turns back into drops, we say it ____.
items.why: Condensation is vapour turning back into liquid drops. It happens on cold things, and high in the sky where clouds form.

items.p: A wet handprint on a sunny tile disappears. Where did the water go?
opts: Into the air, as invisible water vapour
items.why: The water evaporated into the air. Tiles have almost no holes, so it did not soak in. Picking 'destroyed' means thinking water can vanish. It only changes form and moves.
items.context: This question is about The Vanishing Handprint, where you pressed a wet hand on a sunny tile and watched the print fade.

items.p: What is a cloud made of?
opts: Billions of tiny drops of water or ice crystals
items.why: Clouds are tiny drops or ice. Water vapour is invisible, so a cloud we can see cannot be made of vapour alone. Picking 'vapour' is the most common mix-up, even among grown-ups.

items.p: Put the steps of the water cycle in order, starting from the sea.
items: The Sun warms the sea
Water evaporates as invisible vapour
Vapour cools high up and condenses into a cloud
Drops grow heavy and fall as rain
Rain flows in rivers back to the sea
items.why: Warmth makes water evaporate. Rising vapour cools and condenses into cloud drops. They grow and fall. Rivers carry the water back to the sea, and it starts again.

items.p: Water only evaporates when it boils.
items.why: False. Puddles and wet clothes dry on cool days too. Water evaporates at any temperature. Heat just makes it faster.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: water going up into the air as vapour
water falling from clouds as rain, hail or snow
plants giving off water from their leaves
items.why: These are four steps of the water cycle. Each has its own long name, but each describes something you can see.

items.p: A steel tumbler of ice gets wet on the outside. Where do the drops come from?
opts: From the air: vapour condenses on the cold steel
The water leaks through the steel
The ice melts through the steel
items.why: The drops are clear and not salty, though the water inside was coloured and salty. So they came from the air. Picking 'leaks' is very common. But steel has no holes for water to get through.
items.context: This question is about The Cold Tumbler, where you filled a steel tumbler with ice and coloured, salty water.

items.p: Sort these. Is it evaporation or condensation?
items: wet clothes drying on a line
Evaporation
dew on the grass at dawn
Condensation
a puddle shrinking in the sun
Evaporation
drops under a lid on a pot of dal
Condensation
mist on a mirror after a bath
Condensation
a wet floor drying after mopping
Evaporation
items.why: Evaporation is water going into the air, so things dry. Condensation is water coming out of the air, so things get wet.

items.p: Why is rain water not salty, when most of it rose from the salty sea?
opts: Only water evaporates. The salt stays in the sea.
items.why: Salt cannot evaporate at these temperatures, so only fresh water rises. Picking 'clouds filter it' means thinking of a cloud like a sieve. The salt never got to the cloud at all.

items.p: Which will dry fastest?
opts: A wet shirt spread on a line in sun and wind
A wet shirt rolled up in a bucket in the shade
A wet shirt folded in a closed bathroom
items.why: Sun gives energy, wind blows the vapour away, and spreading out gives more surface. All three speed up evaporation. Rolled or folded shirts have very little surface open to the air.

items.p: A season of wet winds from the sea that brings heavy rain to most of India from June to September is called the ____.
items.why: The monsoon brings most of India's rain in about four months.

items.p: Plants put water into the air through their leaves.
items.why: True. This is transpiration. A bag tied over a leafy branch fills with mist and drops.

items.p: Draw or write the water cycle. Use the words evaporate, condense and rain. Use arrows.
items.a: Any drawing or writing that shows water rising from the sea or land as vapour, condensing into a cloud, and falling as rain back to the land and the sea. For example: the Sun warms the sea, water evaporates, it condenses into a cloud, it rains on the hills, and a river carries it back to the sea.
items.why: A good answer goes all the way round and comes back to where it started.

items.p: Name two places at home where you have seen condensation. Say what was cold in each one.
items.a: Any two good examples. For example: the outside of a cold water bottle from the fridge, which was cold. The bathroom mirror after a hot bath, which was cooler than the steamy air.
items.why: Condensation happens where vapour meets something colder.

items.p: Look at the chart from the Evaporation Race. Which place made water evaporate fastest?
opts: The narrow glass in the shade
items.why: The sun's bar is shortest, at 40 minutes. A short bar means the water vanished quickly. Picking the glass usually means reading the tallest bar as the winner. Here, the tallest bar took longest.
items.context: This question is about the Evaporation Race. You put 2 teaspoons of water in four places and timed how long each took to dry.

chart.title: Made-up example results: minutes until each puddle was dry

items.p: In the Evaporation Race, the shade plate took 120 minutes to dry and the sunny plate took 40 minutes. The shade plate took ____ times as long.
items.why: 120 divided by 40 is 3. You can check: 40 + 40 + 40 = 120.
items.context: This question is about the Evaporation Race, where you timed how long 2 teaspoons of water took to dry in different places.

items.p: In the Evaporation Race, the plate in the shade and the narrow glass in the shade had the same water and the same air. Why did the glass take much longer?
opts: Less water was at the top, open to the air
The glass had more water in it
items.why: Water evaporates from its top surface. A wide plate spreads the water out, so much more of it is at the top. Picking 'more water' misses the fair test: both had exactly 2 teaspoons.
items.context: This question is about the Evaporation Race, where 2 teaspoons of water went on a plate and into a narrow glass, side by side in the shade.

items.p: In the Cloud in a Jar, the cloud was much thicker with smoke from an agarbatti. Why?
opts: The vapour condensed onto the smoke specks
The smoke made the jar warmer
items.why: Vapour needs a speck to make a drop. More specks means more drops and a thicker cloud. Real clouds form on dust, salt and smoke. Picking 'smoke is water' mixes up the seed with the drop.
items.context: This question is about A Cloud in a Jar. You made a cloud with warm water and an icy plate, with and without a little smoke.

items.p: The white mist that puffs out of a pressure cooker whistle is…
opts: Tiny drops of water, a little cloud
items.why: Real steam is invisible. As soon as it meets cooler air, it condenses into tiny drops, and those drops are what you see. Picking 'invisible vapour' is close. That vapour is there too, right at the whistle, but you can't see it.

items.p: Sort these. Which part of the water cycle is it?
items: a neem tree on a hot day
Water going up
hail in a summer storm
Water coming down
the sea under the hot Sun
Water going up
snow on a Himalayan peak
Water coming down
wet clothes on a terrace
Water going up
monsoon rain on the Western Ghats
Water coming down
items.why: Trees, the sea and wet clothes give water vapour to the air. Hail, snow and rain bring water back down.

items.p: Mumbai gets about three times as much rain as Pune, though they are close. Why?
opts: Wet winds drop most of their rain on the Western Ghats before reaching Pune
Pune is further from the Sun
Pune's clouds are made of dust
items.why: Wet sea air is pushed up the Western Ghats, cools and rains on the sea side. Little water is left for the far side, the rain shadow. Picking 'further from the Sun' is a common guess, but the distance makes no difference here.

items.p: Raindrops are shaped like teardrops.
items.why: False. Small raindrops are round. Bigger ones are flattened at the bottom, like a burger bun. The teardrop shape only appears as a drop clings to a tap.

items.p: In the leaf-in-a-bag experiment, why did we tie an empty bag next to the leafy one?
opts: To check that the water came from the leaves, not from the air
items.why: The empty bag is the control. It stayed dry, so the water must have come from the leaves. Without it, you could not be sure.
items.context: This question is about Leaves in a Bag, where you tied a clear bag over a leafy branch and an empty bag beside it.

items.p: Match each place to about how long water usually stays there.
pairs: up to hundreds of thousands of years
items.why: Water rushes through the air but waits a very long time in the sea and in ice.

items.p: A small puffy cloud shrinks and vanishes in 10 minutes. Did it rain?
opts: No, its drops evaporated back into the air
No, the cloud floated into space
items.why: Most clouds never rain. Their drops evaporate at the edges, and if they evaporate faster than new drops form, the cloud vanishes. Picking 'it rained' means thinking every cloud must rain.
items.context: This question is about Cloud Watch, where you drew one small cloud three times over 10 minutes.

items.p: On a cold, clear night, water from the air condenses on grass and leaves. In the morning we call these drops ____.
items.why: Dew forms by condensation on cool surfaces at night, and evaporates when the Sun warms them.

items.p: Where does a big thundercloud get the energy to grow so tall?
opts: From vapour condensing into drops, which gives out heat
items.why: The Sun's energy went into the water when it evaporated. When the vapour condenses in the cloud, that energy comes out as heat. Warm air rises, so the cloud grows taller. Picking lightning gets it backwards: the cloud makes the lightning.

items.p: Your solar still made fresh water from salty water. Explain how, using the words evaporate and condense.
items.a: The Sun warmed the salty water, and some of it evaporated into the air in the bowl. The salt stayed behind. The vapour touched the cooler cling film and condensed into fresh drops. They ran down to the low point and dripped into the cup.
items.why: A good answer says that only the water rose, and that it turned back into drops on the cool film.
items.context: This question is about Sea in a Bowl, where you made fresh water from salty water with a bowl, a cup, cling film and sunshine.

items.p: A farmer is glad when the monsoon comes, but a family in a city is worried. Why might they feel differently about the same rain?
items.a: For example: the farmer needs rain to grow rice and fill the wells. The city family worries because streets made of cement and tar cannot soak up the rain, so their road may flood.
items.why: Any answer that gives a reason for each person is good. The same rain can help or hurt, depending on the land it falls on.

worksheets.title: Water Cycle Puzzles and Big Ideas (challenge)

items.p: Rain often falls out of warm monsoon clouds faster than scientists' older ideas can explain. What is one new idea being studied?
opts: Swirling, bumpy air throws drops together more often
The drops are pulled down by the Moon
items.why: Scientists think turbulence, swirling air inside clouds, may make tiny drops bump and join much faster. They are still testing this. Picking the Moon mixes this up with the tides.

items.p: In 1880, John Aitken filtered all the dust out of air in a jar. What happened when he tried to make a cloud?
items.why: Without specks to condense on, vapour could not easily make drops. This showed that clouds need dust, salt or smoke. Picking 'thicker' is a natural guess, because clean air sounds better. But with no specks, the vapour had nothing to condense on.

items.p: A puffy white cloud weighs almost nothing.
items.why: False. Peggy LeMone, a cloud scientist, worked out that an ordinary puffy cloud holds about 500,000 kilograms of water. That is as heavy as about 100 elephants. It floats because its drops are tiny and spread over a huge space, and rising air holds them up.

items.p: About how many cloud drops join to make one raindrop?
items.why: A raindrop is about 100 times wider than a cloud drop. A drop 100 times wider holds 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 times as much water. Picking 'a hundred' only counts the width, not the whole size.

items.p: Pierre Perrault measured the rain around the river Seine in the 1670s. He found the rain was about six times what the river carried. What did this prove?
opts: Rain is more than enough to feed rivers
Rivers are fed by the sea underground
Most rain falls into the sea
items.why: If the rain is six times what the river carries, the river does not need any secret sea water. The rest of the rain soaks in, evaporates or is drunk by plants. Picking 'fed by the sea' was the old belief that Perrault's numbers overturned.

items.p: On Titan, Saturn's biggest moon, what falls as rain?
items.why: Titan is about 180 degrees below zero, so water is hard ice there. Methane is a liquid at that cold, and it rains, fills rivers and makes lakes. Picking sulphuric acid mixes Titan up with Venus.

items.p: Warmer air can hold more water vapour. What does this mean for heavy rain as the world warms?
items.why: More vapour in the air means more water to fall when it rains. Studies of central India since 1950 found days of very heavy rain had become about three times more common. Picking 'stop raining' gets it backwards.

items.p: Some people say forests 'pull' rain inland from the sea. Others say forests only recycle rain that already came. Design a way to find out which is right.
items.a: For example: compare the rain in places just inland from the sea that have forests with similar places without forests, over many years. Or measure how much vapour comes from the trees and where the wind carries it. A fair test changes only the forest, and keeps the distance from the sea and the mountains the same.
items.why: A good answer compares places that differ in only one thing, the forest.

items.p: A drop of water stays in the air for about 9 days, and in the deep sea for about 3,000 years. Why so different?
opts: The sea is huge and the water leaves it slowly. The air holds little water, and it rains out fast.
The Sun does not shine on the deep sea
items.why: The time a drop stays depends on how much water a place holds and how fast it flows out. The air holds very little and lets it go quickly. The sea holds a lot and loses it slowly, mostly from its top.

items.p: Sort these statements about the water cycle.
items: clouds are made of tiny drops, not vapour
Settled: scientists agree
how drops grow into rain so fast in warm clouds
Still argued about
rain is fresh because salt does not evaporate
Settled: scientists agree
whether forests pull rain in from the sea
Still argued about
how much bacteria in clouds help make snow
Still argued about
the Sun's energy drives evaporation
Settled: scientists agree
items.why: Science has a settled middle and an open edge. Knowing which is which is part of thinking like a scientist.

items.p: Most water cycle pictures show only sea, clouds, rain and rivers. What did scientists in 2019 say was missing?
opts: People: dams, borewells, farms and cities
items.why: People now move huge amounts of water, but most pictures leave us out. Picking fish is a reasonable thought, since animals are part of the cycle too. But the big missing piece was people.

items.p: Heraclitus, a thinker in ancient Greece, said that new waters keep flowing past people stepping into the same river. Is a river the same river from one day to the next? Give a reason for each side.
items.a: A balanced answer. For example: yes, because its banks, its name and its path stay the same. No, because all of its water is different water from yesterday.
items.why: There is no single right answer. What counts is giving a reason for each side.

items.p: Is a cloud a thing, or something that keeps happening? Use something you saw in this unit.
items.a: For example: a cloud is something happening, because in Cloud Watch my cloud kept changing and then vanished, and in the jar it formed and disappeared in a minute. Or: it is a thing, because I can see it, name it and draw it.
items.why: Any answer with a reason from what you saw is good.

items.p: In the jar garden project, you closed the lid and never watered it, yet the plants lived. Why?
opts: The same water kept going round: evaporating, condensing and dripping back into the soil
Water came in through the glass
items.why: The jar is a closed water cycle. Water evaporates from the soil, leaves give off vapour, it condenses on the glass and runs back down. The Earth works in a similar way.
items.context: This question is about A Rain Forest in a Jar, a closed jar garden you built and did not water for two weeks.

items.p: Draw a mountain with the sea on one side. Show the wet wind, the clouds, where the rain falls, and the dry rain shadow. Label each part.
items.a: The wind blows from the sea up the near slope. Clouds and rain are on the sea side. The far side is dry and labelled rain shadow.
items.why: Wet air cools as it rises up the mountain, so it rains on the sea side. Little water is left for the far side.

experiments.title: Sea in a Bowl: fresh water from salty water
experiments.question: Can sunshine turn salty water into fresh water we could drink?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the drops form on the cling film, will they taste salty, a little salty, or not salty at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same salty water for everything. Taste a tiny drop of the salty water at the start, so you can compare. Collect the drops only from the cup, not from the bowl.
results_table: What I see on the cling film
How much water is in the cup

materials.item: a big wide bowl, steel or glass, as big as you have
a small, heavy cup or katori that is shorter than the bowl
cling film, enough to cover the bowl, or a clear plastic bag cut open
a small pebble or a coin
2 teaspoons of salt and 2 cups of warm water
a sunny spot for 3 to 4 hours, from late morning

experiments.safety: Use clean dishes, so the water is safe to taste. Taste only a drop or two. Do not drink the salty water. Glass bowls get hot in the sun, so a grown-up should lift them.

schedule.what: Set up the still in the morning (10 minutes). Look at it after 30 minutes (5 minutes). Collect and taste the water after 3 to 4 hours (15 minutes).

experiments.record: Fill in the table at the start, after 30 minutes and at the end. Draw your still, with arrows showing where the water went.
experiments.context: This is an experiment about why rain is fresh. You make a solar still, a simple machine that uses sunshine to get fresh water from salty water.

flow.do: 1. Stir 2 teaspoons of salt into 2 cups of warm water until it disappears. 2. Let your child taste one drop on a fingertip. 3. Pour all the salty water into the big bowl.
flow.say: This is our sea. Taste one tiny drop. Salty, isn't it? Real sea water is even saltier, about 6 teaspoons in every litre.
flow.kid: Stir 2 spoons of salt into 2 cups of warm water. Taste one tiny drop. Salty! Pour it into the big bowl. This is your sea.

ask.q: Where do you think the salt went when you stirred it?
good: It dissolved. It is still in the water, in pieces too small to see.
It is hiding in the water.

flow.context: This is the first step of Sea in a Bowl. You make salty 'sea' water and taste it, so you can compare later.

flow.do: 1. Stand the small cup in the middle of the bowl. Its rim must be above the salty water, and no salty water may get in. 2. Stretch cling film tightly over the bowl and seal the edges. 3. Put the pebble on the film, right above the cup, so the film dips down to a point. 4. Put the bowl in full sun.
flow.say: The Sun will warm our sea. Watch the cling film. The pebble makes a low point, right over the cup. Why do you think we put it there?
flow.kid: Put the small cup in the middle. Cover the bowl tightly with cling film. Put a pebble on top, over the cup. Put it in the sun.
flow.parent: Late morning to mid-afternoon on a sunny day works best. A dark bowl, warm water and a tight seal all help. The film must dip down over the cup but not touch the water.

flow.do: After about 30 minutes, look closely at the underside of the cling film. Do not open it.
flow.say: Look underneath the film. What do you see? Where did those drops come from?
flow.kid: After 30 minutes, look under the film. Do not open it! What do you see?
flow.wait: Leave the still in the sun for 3 to 4 hours.

check.q: Drops have formed on the underside of the cling film over the bowl. Where did they come from?
options: Water evaporated from the bowl and condensed on the film
The cling film leaked
Rain fell on it
check.why: The Sun warmed the salty water, and some of it evaporated into the air inside the bowl. When the vapour touched the cooler film, it condensed into drops. Picking 'leaked' usually means thinking the water came through the film. It came from below.

flow.do: 1. After 3 to 4 hours, tap the film gently. The last drops run down to the point and drip into the cup. 2. Peel back the film carefully. 3. Lift out the cup without spilling any salty water into it. 4. Each person tastes one drop from the cup.
flow.say: Let's taste the water in the cup. Remember, the sea water was salty. Is this?
flow.kid: Tap the film so the drops fall in the cup. Lift the cup out carefully. Taste one drop. Is it salty?
flow.parent: On a hot, sunny day, you may get one to four teaspoons in the cup. It should taste of plain water. If it tastes salty, some salty water splashed into the cup, so try again more carefully. Is the day cloudy? Then a grown-up sets the bowl over a pan of hot water. Put a bag of ice cubes on the film in place of the pebble. Drops form within 10 minutes.

check.q: In the Sea in a Bowl experiment, the water in the cup does not taste salty. Why?
options: Only the water evaporated. The salt stayed in the bowl.
The Sun burned up the salt
The cling film filtered out the salt
check.why: Salt cannot evaporate at these temperatures. Only water rose as vapour, and it condensed as fresh drops. The salt is still in the bowl. Picking 'burned up' means thinking the salt is destroyed. Picking 'filtered' means thinking the film is like a sieve. The water never went through the film. It rose, then dripped down.

flow.do: Compare your still with the real water cycle. Point to each part.
flow.say: The salty water is the sea. The Sun is the Sun. The film is like the cold sky, and the drops are like clouds. The drips into the cup are rain. Rain is fresh for the same reason.
flow.kid: Your bowl is the sea. The film is the cold sky. The drops are a cloud. The drips are rain. That is why rain is not salty!
flow.think: Sea water is salty, but rain is fresh. Where does the salt that stays behind in the sea come from?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: sunshine can make fresh water from salty water. What I saw: drops formed on the film after 30 minutes, and the water in the cup did not taste salty, though the bowl water did. Why: only the water evaporated, and the salt stayed behind in the bowl.

setup.caption: 1. Pour salty water into a big bowl. Stand a small cup in the middle.

setup.art: Cling film stretched over the bowl with a pebble in the middle making it dip down over the cup, the bowl sitting in bright sunshine.
setup.caption: 2. Cover with cling film. Put a pebble on top, over the cup. Leave it in the sun.

setup.art: Close-up of drops on the underside of the cling film running down to the low point and dripping into the cup.
setup.caption: 3. Drops form on the film, run down and drip into the cup.

setup.art: A child tasting a drop from the cup with a surprised smile, the bowl of salty water beside them.
setup.caption: 4. Taste a drop from the cup. Is it salty?

experiments.title: A Cloud in a Jar
experiments.question: What does it take to make a cloud?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a cloud form better with smoke in the jar, or without smoke? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Do it twice. Keep everything the same, the same jar, the same amount of hot water and the same ice, but change only one thing: smoke or no smoke. Look at the jar against a dark cloth both times.
results_table: How thick was the cloud: none, thin or thick?
What happened when I lifted the lid?

materials.item: a clear glass jar, as big as a jam jar or bigger
hot water from a kettle or a pan, left to cool for 2 minutes, about 3 fingers deep in the jar
a steel plate or the jar's metal lid, turned upside down
6 to 8 ice cubes
an agarbatti, an incense stick, or a matchstick, lit by a grown-up
a dark cloth or dark paper, and a torch if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and lights the agarbatti or match. Very hot water can crack thin glass, so let it cool for 2 minutes first, and stand the jar on a cloth. Do it near an open window.

schedule.what: Make a cloud without smoke, then with smoke. Compare them.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for both tries. Draw the jar with the cloud, and label the warm water, the vapour, the cold lid and the smoke specks.
experiments.context: This is an experiment about how clouds form. You make a real cloud inside a jar, using warm water, cold ice and a little smoke.

flow.do: 1. Hang the dark cloth behind the jar. 2. A grown-up pours hot water into the jar, about 3 fingers deep. 3. Swirl it gently so the warm water wets the sides. 4. Put the steel plate on top with the ice cubes on it.
flow.say: The warm water is our sea on a hot day. The ice on top is the cold sky, high up. Watch the top of the jar carefully.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to pour hot water into the jar. Put the steel plate on top. Put ice on the plate. Watch the top of the jar.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Cloud in a Jar. You set up warm water below and cold ice above, like the sea and the sky.

flow.do: Watch for 1 minute. Shine a torch through the side if you have one. Note how thick the mist is.
flow.say: Do you see a little mist under the plate? Is it thick or thin?
flow.kid: Watch for one minute. Shine a torch through the side. Is there mist? Is it thick or thin?
flow.parent: You may see a thin mist, or drops on the underside of the plate. That is fine. The next step usually makes it much thicker.

flow.do: 1. Empty the jar and start again with fresh hot water. 2. A grown-up lights the agarbatti or a match, then blows it out. Hold the smoking end inside the jar for 3 seconds. 3. Put the plate and ice back on quickly.
flow.say: Now we'll add smoke. Smoke is made of billions of tiny specks. Watch what the vapour does now.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to put a little smoke in the jar. Put the plate and ice back on fast. Watch!
flow.parent: Within about 30 seconds, a white swirling cloud usually forms under the plate. The dark cloth and a torch beam make it much easier to see. If nothing shows, the water may have cooled: start again with hotter water.

flow.do: Lift the plate off and watch the cloud float out of the jar.
flow.say: Let's let our cloud go. Watch it. Where does it go after it leaves the jar?
flow.kid: Lift the plate. Your cloud floats out! Watch it. Where does it go?

check.q: In the Cloud in a Jar experiment, why did the smoke make a thicker cloud?
options: Vapour condensed onto the tiny smoke specks, making many more drops
Smoke is a kind of cloud
The smoke made the water hotter
check.why: Water vapour needs something to stick to before it can make a drop. Each smoke speck becomes the seed of one tiny drop. More specks means more drops, and a thicker cloud. Real clouds form on specks of dust, salt and smoke. Picking 'smoke is a cloud' mixes up the seeds with the drops.

flow.think: The cloud vanished when it left the jar. Did its water disappear, or go somewhere?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a cloud needs warm water vapour, cold air, and tiny specks to form on. What I saw: without smoke there was only a thin mist, but with smoke a thick white cloud formed in about 30 seconds. Why: the vapour cooled under the icy plate and condensed onto the smoke specks, making millions of tiny drops.

setup.caption: 1. A grown-up pours warm water into the jar.

setup.art: A smoking, blown-out agarbatti held inside the mouth of the jar for a moment.
setup.caption: 2. Add a little smoke from a blown-out agarbatti.

setup.caption: 3. Put a plate of ice on top. Watch a cloud form.

setup.art: A hand lifting the plate as a wisp of white cloud floats up out of the jar.
setup.caption: 4. Lift the plate and let your cloud go.

experiments.title: Leaves in a Bag: do plants give off water?
experiments.question: Do plants put water into the air?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you tie a clear bag over a leafy branch, will water appear inside it? Will it appear in an empty bag tied up in the same place? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two bags of the same kind. Tie one over a leafy branch. Seal the other with only air inside, and tie it to a bare stick or a bare branch next to the first. Leave both in the same sunny place for the same time.

materials.item: 2 clear plastic bags, such as zip bags or clean food bags
2 rubber bands or pieces of string
a leafy plant in the sun: a bush, a small tree, or a big potted plant like a money plant or hibiscus
a teaspoon
a clock or phone to check the time

experiments.safety: Be gentle with the plant. Choose a branch with healthy leaves. Take the bag off after 3 to 4 hours, so the leaves do not get too hot.

schedule.what: Tie on the bags in the morning (8 minutes). Check after 1 hour (4 minutes). Collect the water after 3 hours (8 minutes).

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the branch in its bag, with arrows showing water going up the stem and out of the leaves.
experiments.context: This is an experiment about plants and the water cycle. You tie a clear bag over a leafy branch to see if leaves give off water.

flow.do: 1. Water the plant well, an hour before you start if you can. 2. Choose a leafy branch in the sun. 3. Slip a clear bag over 8 to 10 leaves. 4. Tie it gently but tightly around the stem with a rubber band. 5. Seal the second bag with only air inside and tie it to a bare stick beside the plant.
flow.say: We'll catch anything that comes out of these leaves. The empty bag is our 'control'. It shows what happens with no leaves at all.
flow.kid: Slip a clear bag over a leafy branch. Tie it gently. Tie an empty bag next to it. That one is for comparing.

ask.q: Why do we need the empty bag too?
good: To check the water comes from the leaves, not from the air.

flow.context: This is the first step of Leaves in a Bag. You tie a clear bag over a leafy branch, and an empty bag beside it to compare.

flow.do: After about 1 hour, look at both bags. Do not open them.
flow.say: Look at the bag on the leaves. Is it misty? Now look at the empty bag. What's different?
flow.kid: After one hour, look at both bags. Which one is misty inside?
flow.parent: On a sunny day the leaf bag usually turns misty within an hour. The empty bag stays clear. On a cool or cloudy day it may take two or three hours.

flow.do: 1. After about 3 hours, tap the leaf bag so the drops run to the bottom. 2. Untie it carefully and tip the water into a teaspoon. 3. Count how many teaspoons you collect. 4. Take both bags off the plant.
flow.say: Let's see how much water this one branch gave off. Imagine the whole tree doing this.
flow.kid: Tap the bag. Untie it carefully. Pour the water into a spoon. How much did you get?
flow.parent: A branch of a bush or tree in the sun often gives a teaspoon or more in 3 hours. A small pot plant may give only a few drops. That is still a result. If there are no drops at all, the plant may be thirsty, so water it and try again the next day.

check.q: In the leaf-in-a-bag experiment, water collected in the bag on the leaves, but not in the empty bag. Where did the water come from?
options: From the leaves: water came up from the roots and left the leaves as vapour
From the air outside the bag
From rain
check.why: The empty bag stayed dry, so the water did not come from the air trapped in a bag. It came out of the leaves. Water travels up from the roots and leaves through tiny holes, as vapour. It condensed on the bag. This is called transpiration.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants give off water into the air. What I saw: the bag on the leaves went misty in one hour and I collected about one teaspoon of water, but the empty bag stayed dry. Why: water goes up from the roots and leaves through tiny holes in the leaves as vapour. This is transpiration.

experiments.title: The Cold Tumbler: where do the drops come from?
experiments.question: When a cold tumbler gets wet on the outside, where does the water come from?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If we put coloured water and ice inside a steel tumbler, what colour will the drops on the outside be? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two tumblers of the same kind, side by side. Fill one with ice and coloured water. Fill the other with the same amount of coloured water at room temperature. Wipe both dry and check them after the same time.
results_table: Wet or dry outside after 5 minutes?
Colour of the drops on the outside
Taste of the drops: plain or salty?

materials.item: 2 steel tumblers of the same kind
ice cubes, enough to half fill one tumbler
a few drops of food colour, or a pinch of haldi
a pinch of salt
a dry cloth or tissue

experiments.safety: Safe to do alone. Taste only drops from the outside of a clean tumbler.

schedule.what: Fill the two tumblers, wait 5 minutes, and compare the outsides.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the cold tumbler, with arrows showing water coming from the air onto it.
experiments.context: This is an experiment about condensation. A cold steel tumbler gets wet on the outside, and you find out whether the water leaked through or came from the air.

flow.do: 1. Stir a few drops of food colour, or a pinch of haldi, into a jug of water. 2. Fill tumbler A half with ice, then top it up with the coloured water. 3. Fill tumbler B with the coloured water only. 4. Stir a pinch of salt into both. 5. Wipe the outsides completely dry.
flow.say: Both tumblers have the same coloured, salty water. Only one is cold. Watch the outsides.
flow.kid: Colour some water with haldi. Fill one tumbler with ice and coloured water. Fill the other with just coloured water. Add a pinch of salt to both. Wipe them dry.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Cold Tumbler. You fill two steel tumblers with the same coloured water, but only one gets ice.

flow.do: Wait 5 minutes. Then run a dry fingertip down the outside of each tumbler. Look at the drops and wipe some onto white paper.
flow.say: Which tumbler is wet on the outside? What colour are the drops on the paper?
flow.kid: Wait 5 minutes. Run a finger down each tumbler. Which is wet? Wipe a drop on white paper. What colour is it?
flow.parent: On a humid day, the cold tumbler gets covered in drops within a minute or two. On a very dry winter day there may be only a little mist. Then breathe on it, and watch the mist appear. The drops on the paper will be clear, not yellow or coloured.

flow.do: Let your child taste one drop from the outside of the cold tumbler.
flow.say: The water inside is salty. Taste a drop from the outside. Is it salty too?
flow.kid: Taste one drop from the outside of the cold tumbler. Is it salty, like the inside?

check.q: In the Cold Tumbler experiment, the drops on the outside are clear and not salty, though the water inside is yellow and salty. Where did they come from?
options: Water vapour in the air condensed on the cold tumbler
The water leaked through the steel
The ice melted through the steel
check.why: If the drops had leaked through, they would be yellow and salty, like the water inside. They are clear and plain. So they came from the air. Invisible water vapour touched the cold steel, cooled and turned into drops. That is condensation. The warm tumbler stayed dry, because it was not cold enough.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the drops on a cold tumbler come out of the air. What I saw: only the tumbler with ice got wet outside, and its drops were clear and not salty, while the water inside was yellow and salty. Why: invisible water vapour in the air condensed on the cold steel.

experiments.title: The Evaporation Race
experiments.question: What makes water evaporate faster: sunshine, wind, or a wide surface?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the four places in order, from the one that will dry first to the one that will dry last: sun, shade, fan, narrow glass in the shade. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Put exactly the same amount of water in each, 2 teaspoons. Use three identical steel plates and one narrow glass. Start them all at the same time. Change only one thing for each: sun, shade, wind from a fan, or a narrow container.

materials.item: 3 identical steel plates
1 narrow glass or tumbler
a teaspoon
a sunny spot, a shady spot, and a fan in the shade
a clock or phone to check the time

experiments.safety: Keep fingers away from the fan. Put the plates where nobody will step on them.

schedule.what: Set up the race (8 minutes). Check every 15 minutes for 2 to 3 hours, one minute each time (12 minutes). Make the bar chart and talk (10 minutes).

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each place. Make each bar as tall as its number of minutes.
experiments.context: This is a race between four puddles of water. You find out what makes water evaporate, or dry up, fastest.

flow.do: 1. Put exactly 2 teaspoons of water on each plate and into the glass. 2. Put plate 1 in the sun. Put plate 2 in the shade. Put plate 3 in the shade, in front of a fan. 3. Put the glass in the shade next to plate 2. 4. Write down the start time.
flow.say: This is a race. The winner is the puddle that disappears first. Which one will win?
flow.kid: Put 2 spoons of water on each plate, and in the glass. One in the sun. One in the shade. One by a fan. The glass in the shade. Go!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Evaporation Race. You put the same amount of water in four places to see which dries first.

flow.do: 1. Check every 15 minutes. 2. When a plate is completely dry, write down the time. 3. Work out the minutes it took. 4. If the glass still has water after 3 hours, write 'more than 180 minutes'.
flow.say: Let's check our race. Has any puddle gone yet? Where do you think its water went?
flow.kid: Check every 15 minutes. When a plate is dry, write down the time. Is the glass dry yet?
flow.parent: On a hot summer day, the sunny plate often dries in about 30 to 45 minutes. The fan plate is usually next, and the shade plate takes much longer. The narrow glass usually takes the longest, often until the next day. In cool or humid weather everything is slower, so use 1 teaspoon instead.

chart.title: Made-up example results: minutes until each puddle was dry
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart, with one bar for each place.
flow.say: Each place gets one bar. The taller the bar, the longer that water took to evaporate. Which bar is the shortest?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each place. Make it as tall as its minutes. The shortest bar won the race!

check.q: In the Evaporation Race bar chart, the shortest bar shows the place where water…
options: Evaporated fastest
Evaporated slowest
Did not evaporate
check.why: The bar shows how many minutes the water took to disappear. A short bar means only a few minutes, so that water evaporated fastest. Picking 'slowest' usually means reading a short bar as a small amount of evaporation. Here, short means quick.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: sunshine, wind and a wide surface all make water evaporate faster. What I saw: the sunny plate dried in 40 minutes, the fan plate in 60, the shade plate in 120, and the glass took more than 3 hours. Why: heat makes water molecules jiggle faster so more escape, wind blows them away, and a wide puddle has a bigger surface for them to escape from.

activities.title: The Vanishing Handprint

materials.item: a bowl of water
a dry floor tile, a stone step or a slate in the sun
a steel plate, or a mirror, cooled in the fridge for 5 minutes if you can

activities.safety: Wet tiles are slippery. Do this on a step or a patch of floor where nobody is walking.

schedule.what: Make wet handprints in the sun and in the shade, then breathe on a cold plate. Notice and wonder.

activities.record: Draw your handprint at the start and after one minute. Write one thing you noticed and one thing you wonder.
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity to start the unit. You watch a wet handprint vanish, and breathe a little cloud onto a cold plate.

flow.do: 1. Dip your child's hand in water and shake it once. 2. Press it flat on a dry tile in the sun. 3. Make a second print on a tile in the shade. 4. Count slowly together and watch both prints.
flow.say: Let's watch your handprints. Which one starts to fade first? Watch the fingers and the edges.
flow.kid: Wet your hand. Press it on a tile in the sun. Press it again in the shade. Count slowly. Which print fades first?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Vanishing Handprint. You press wet handprints on tiles in the sun and the shade, and watch them fade.

flow.do: When the sunny print has gone, ask where the water went. Do not explain yet. Collect all the ideas.
flow.say: The water didn't soak into the tile. Where did it go? Any idea is a good idea for now.
flow.kid: Your handprint has gone. It did not soak in. Where did the water go? Say your best guess.
flow.parent: Children often say it went into the tile, it disappeared, or the Sun ate it. Just listen and write their ideas down. The unit will answer them. The water evaporated: it went into the air as invisible vapour.

flow.do: 1. Hold the cool steel plate close to your child's mouth. 2. Ask them to breathe out slowly onto it, like a sigh. 3. Watch the mist appear and vanish.
flow.say: Breathe on the plate. A little cloud! Where did that water come from? And now, where is it going?
flow.kid: Breathe out slowly on the cold plate. See the mist? Now watch it go. Where did it come from?

check.q: You breathe on a cold steel plate and it mists up. Where did the water come from?
options: From your breath: there is invisible water vapour in it
From the steel
From the air conditioner
check.why: Your breath has invisible water vapour in it. When it touches the cold plate, it cools and turns into tiny drops, which you see as mist. That is condensation. A few seconds later, the drops evaporate back into the air.

flow.think: The handprint went into the air. The breath came out of the air onto the plate. Are these two the same thing, going opposite ways?

setup.caption: 1. Press a wet handprint on a tile in the sun, and one in the shade.

setup.art: Two tiles side by side: the sunny one dry, the shady one still showing a faint handprint.
setup.caption: 2. Watch which one disappears first.

setup.art: A child breathing a small misty patch onto a steel plate held near their face.
setup.caption: 3. Breathe on a cold steel plate. Watch the mist come and go.

activities.title: The Morning Dew Walk

materials.item: a torch or phone light
a small dark cloth or a piece of black paper
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Wear chappals, as grass is slippery when wet.

schedule.what: Go out just after sunrise and look for dew.
Go back to the same places 2 hours later. Is the dew still there?

activities.record: List 5 places where you found dew. Then write which ones were dry 2 hours later.
activities.context: This is a walk at sunrise to find dew, the water that comes out of the air onto cool things at night, and to see it evaporate again. Do it if you have grass, plants or parked cars outside your home.

flow.do: 1. Go out just after sunrise. 2. Look for drops on grass, leaves, spider webs, car windscreens and railings. 3. Wipe a car window or a leaf with the dark cloth and look at the wet patch. 4. Shine the torch low across the grass to make drops sparkle.
flow.say: It didn't rain last night. So where did all these drops come from?
flow.kid: Look for drops on grass, leaves, webs and car windows. It did not rain! Where did they come from?
flow.parent: Dew forms best on clear, still nights, especially in winter and just after the monsoon. On a hot, dry summer night, you may find none. Then fill a steel tumbler with ice instead, and watch dew form on it. On a cloudy or windy night, there is less dew.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Morning Dew Walk. You go out at sunrise to look for dew on grass, leaves and cars.

flow.do: Go back to the same places about 2 hours later.
flow.say: Look at the same leaves now. The dew has gone. Where did it go this time?
flow.kid: Go back to the same places later. Is the dew still there? Where did it go?

check.q: On the dew walk, the grass was wet at sunrise but dry 2 hours later. What happened?
options: The dew came from the air at night, and evaporated back into the air when the Sun warmed it
The dew soaked into the grass and was used up
It rained and then stopped
check.why: At night, grass and leaves cool down, and water vapour from the air condenses on them as dew. In the morning, the Sun warms them, and the dew evaporates back into the air. Picking 'soaked in' is a good guess, but the grass is dry because the water went up, not down.

flow.think: Dew comes out of the air at night and goes back in the morning. What changed: the light, the cold, or both?

activities.title: Cloud Watch: is it growing or shrinking?

materials.item: a place to lie or sit and see the sky: a terrace, a garden or a window
a notebook and pencils
a clock or phone timer

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun, even through clouds. Wear a cap in strong sunshine.

schedule.what: Watch one cloud for 10 minutes, draw it three times, and name the kinds of clouds you can see.

activities.record: Draw one cloud at 0, 5 and 10 minutes. Write whether it grew, shrank or changed shape. Name the kinds of clouds you saw.
activities.context: This is a sky-watching activity. You pick one cloud and watch it closely, to see that clouds are always forming and drying up.

flow.do: Learn three cloud names together. Puffy cauliflower clouds are cumulus. Flat grey sheets are stratus. Thin wispy streaks high up are cirrus.
flow.say: Scientists name clouds by their shape. Cumulus means 'heap'. Stratus means 'layer'. Cirrus means 'curl of hair'. Can you find any of them?
flow.kid: Puffy heaps are cumulus. Flat grey sheets are stratus. Thin wisps high up are cirrus. Can you see any?
flow.parent: Luke Howard, a London chemist who loved watching the sky, gave clouds these Latin names in 1802. People still use them today.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cloud Watch. You learn three cloud names before choosing one cloud to watch.

flow.do: 1. Choose one small puffy cloud. 2. Draw it now. 3. Draw it again after 5 minutes, and after 10 minutes. Use something still, like a tree or a roof, to keep track of where it is.
flow.say: Watch the edges of your cloud. Are they sharp or fuzzy? Is it getting bigger or smaller?
flow.kid: Pick one small puffy cloud. Draw it. Wait 5 minutes and draw it again. Then once more. Is it growing or shrinking?
flow.parent: Small puffy clouds often shrink and vanish in 10 to 15 minutes. Their edges evaporate into drier air. Others grow, because new vapour keeps condensing at the bottom. On a clear day with no clouds, do this activity another day. On a fully grey day, watch for gaps opening and closing instead.

flow.do: Look at the three drawings together.
flow.say: Your cloud changed in just 10 minutes. Was it the same cloud at the end?
flow.kid: Look at your three drawings. Did your cloud change? Is it the same cloud?

check.q: During Cloud Watch, a small cloud shrinks and vanishes in 10 minutes. What happened to its tiny drops?
options: They evaporated into the air as invisible vapour
They fell as rain
They floated up into space
check.why: A small cloud's drops are always evaporating at its edges. If drier air mixes in, they evaporate faster than new drops can form, and the cloud vanishes. Its water is still in the air, as invisible vapour. Picking 'fell as rain' means expecting all clouds to rain. Most clouds dry up without raining at all.

flow.think: If a cloud is always losing drops and making new ones, is it a thing or something that keeps happening?

activities.title: A Rainstorm in the Room: clap and dance the water cycle

materials.item: your hands and feet
a steel plate and a spoon, or a drum, if you have one
space to move

activities.safety: Dance on a mat or a carpet, not on a slippery floor.

schedule.what: Make a rainstorm with sounds, then dance the water cycle.

activities.record: Draw the parts of your dance: rising, floating, gathering, falling and flowing back to the sea.
activities.context: This is a music and dance activity. You make the sound of a rainstorm with your hands, then dance the journey of water from the sea to a cloud and back.

flow.do: Make a rainstorm together, following the leader. 1. Rub palms together: wind. 2. Snap fingers: first drops. 3. Pat your knees: rain. 4. Stamp feet and bang the plate: downpour and thunder. 5. Then go back down in the opposite order, until there is silence.
flow.say: Copy me. First the wind. Then the first drops. Now the rain is getting heavier. Here comes the downpour! Now it's easing off.
flow.kid: Rub your hands: wind. Snap your fingers: drops. Pat your knees: rain. Stamp your feet: a big storm! Then go back, slowly, to quiet.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Rainstorm in the Room. You make a rainstorm with your hands and feet, from a breeze to a downpour and back.

flow.do: Dance the water cycle in four parts. 1. Crouch low, as water in the sea. 2. Rise slowly with wavy arms: evaporation. 3. Float, drift and gather close to others: a cloud. 4. Leap and drop down: rain. 5. Crawl or slide back to where you started: the river to the sea. Repeat it 2 or 3 times.
flow.say: You are water in the sea. The Sun warms you. Rise up slowly, slowly. Now float as a cloud. Gather together. You're getting heavy. Now fall!
flow.kid: Crouch low as the sea. Rise slowly with wavy arms. Float like a cloud. Gather close. Now leap and fall as rain! Flow back to the sea.

check.q: In the water cycle dance, you rose slowly up from the 'sea'. Which part of the water cycle was that?
options: Evaporation
Rain
A river
check.why: Rising up from the sea is evaporation, when water turns into invisible vapour and goes up into the air. Rain is the falling part of the dance. The river is the part where you flow back to the sea.

flow.do: Sit together quietly and talk.
flow.say: Our storm got louder and louder, then quieter. Real storms do that too. Which part of the dance did you like best?
flow.kid: Sit down. Which part of the dance did you like best? Which part of the water cycle was it?
flow.think: In the dance, you went round and round. Where would the dance end, if it were real water?

activities.title: Make a Monsoon: the kettle and the mountain

materials.item: an electric kettle or a pan of water on the stove
a cold steel plate or tray, chilled in the fridge or freezer for 15 minutes
a kitchen towel to hold the plate
a big map of India, printed or in an atlas
a piece of string or wool, and some sticky notes

activities.safety: Only a grown-up holds the plate near the steam. Steam burns. Children watch from at least an arm's length away.

schedule.what: Make 'monsoon rain' with steam and a cold plate, then trace the monsoon's path across a map of India.

activities.record: On the map, draw arrows for the monsoon winds. Colour the wet sea side of the Western Ghats dark blue, and the rain shadow beyond it light yellow.
activities.context: This activity shows how the monsoon makes rain. Steam meets a cold 'mountain' and turns to drops. Then you trace the monsoon across India on a map.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils the kettle. 2. The grown-up holds the cold plate with a towel. Tilt it in the steam, like the slope of a mountain, about 20 centimetres above the spout. 3. Watch drops gather on the plate and drip off its lower edge.
flow.say: The kettle is the warm sea. The steam is the wet wind. The cold plate is the Western Ghats. Watch what happens when the wet air meets the cold mountain.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to hold a cold plate in the kettle steam. Watch from far away. Drops form and fall! That is rain on the mountains.
flow.parent: Drops form within a few seconds and soon drip. If the plate warms up, swap it for a second cold plate. On real mountains it is not the rock that is cold. Wet air is pushed up the slope, and rising air cools down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make a Monsoon. A grown-up holds a cold plate in kettle steam, to show wet air turning to rain at a mountain.

flow.do: 1. Open the map of India. 2. Lay the string from the Arabian Sea to the Kerala coast. Put a sticky note saying 'about 1 June'. 3. Move the string up the west coast to Mumbai, and on across India to Delhi. 4. Put a sticky note on Mumbai and one on Pune, just over the Western Ghats.
flow.say: The monsoon arrives in Kerala around the first of June. Then it moves north, week by week. It covers all of India by about the eighth of July. Mumbai gets about three times as much rain as Pune. Why do you think?
flow.kid: Lay the string from the sea to Kerala. That is the monsoon arriving, around 1 June. Move it up to Mumbai, then to Delhi. Find Pune, just over the mountains.

ask.q: Why does Pune, just over the mountains, get much less rain than Mumbai?
good: The wet wind drops its rain on the mountains first.
There is not much water left by the time it gets over.

flow.do: Find Meghalaya on the map, in the North-East. Put a sticky note on Mawsynram and Sohra, also called Cherrapunji.
flow.say: Wet winds from the Bay of Bengal hit the hills of Meghalaya and rise steeply. Mawsynram and Sohra get more than 11 metres of rain a year. That is taller than a three-storey building, if it all stayed in one place.
flow.kid: Find Meghalaya. Mawsynram is one of the wettest places on Earth. Its rain in one year would be taller than a three-storey house!

check.q: In Make a Monsoon, why did the drops form on the plate held in the steam?
options: The cold plate cooled the vapour, so it condensed into drops
The plate was wet before
The steam made the plate rusty
check.why: Water vapour in the steam touched the cold plate, cooled and turned into drops. That is condensation. On real mountains, wet air is pushed upwards, and rising air cools, so its vapour condenses into clouds and rain.

activities.title: How Long Does a Drop Stay? The washing line of time

materials.item: a long string or a washing line across a room
6 clothes pegs
6 cards to write on
a pencil

schedule.what: Write six cards, guess the order, and peg them on the line from fastest to slowest.

activities.record: Copy the line into your notebook as a strip, with the six places in order.
activities.context: This activity shows how long water usually stays in each part of the water cycle, from a few days in a cloud to thousands of years in the sea.

flow.do: Write one card each for: THE AIR, A RIVER, A PUDDLE, A PLANT, THE DEEP SEA, ANTARCTIC ICE. Ask your child to peg them on the line from the shortest stay to the longest.
flow.say: A drop of water can stay in some places for a short time, and in others for ages. Which do you think is quickest? Which is slowest?
flow.kid: Write six cards: air, river, puddle, plant, deep sea, Antarctic ice. Peg them in order. Shortest stay first.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Long Does a Drop Stay? You guess how long water stays in six places, and peg them in order.

flow.do: Write the real times on the cards and move them into the right order. A puddle: hours or days. A plant: hours to days. The air: about 9 days. A river: weeks to months. The deep sea: about 3,000 years. Antarctic ice: up to hundreds of thousands of years.
flow.say: Water in the air comes down in about 9 days. But a drop in the deep sea may wait 3,000 years. Some ice in Antarctica froze long before there were any modern humans like us.
flow.kid: Now write the real times. Air: about 9 days. Deep sea: about 3,000 years. Antarctic ice: hundreds of thousands of years! Move your cards.
flow.parent: These are rough averages. Scientists compare how much water is in each place with how fast it flows in and out. Scientists have drilled out Antarctic ice about 800,000 years old.

flow.do: Stand at the AIR end of the line, then walk to the ICE end.
flow.say: Rain today was in the air only a week or so ago. But it might have been in the sea for thousands of years before that.
flow.kid: Stand at the air end. Walk to the ice end. That is a very long time for a drop to wait!

check.q: On the washing line of time, where does water usually stay the shortest time?
options: In the air, about 9 days
In the deep sea, about 3,000 years
In Antarctic ice
check.why: Water vapour in the air soon condenses and falls as rain or snow, on average within about 9 days. The sea and the ice hold water for a very long time, because they are so big and the water leaves them slowly.

flow.think: If the air holds water for only 9 days, where does all the water in tomorrow's clouds come from?

projects.title: A Rain Forest in a Jar: a water cycle that runs by itself

materials.item: a big clear glass jar with a lid, at least 1 litre
small pebbles or gravel, about 2 fingers deep
a handful of charcoal from a cooking fire or a shop, crushed (optional, it keeps the jar fresh)
garden soil or potting soil, about 4 fingers deep
2 or 3 small plants that like shade and damp: moss from a wall, a small fern, or a money plant cutting
a spray bottle or a spoon for watering

projects.safety: Wash your hands after touching soil. Only a grown-up handles broken glass if the jar cracks.

schedule.what: Build the jar garden, water it once, close the lid, and put it in bright light but not in direct sun.
Look in the morning and the afternoon. Where are the drops? Draw them.
Check again. Are the plants healthy? Is there mist?
Check again. Has any water been added? Is the soil still damp?
Two weeks without watering. Compare with day 1, and explain the jar's water cycle to someone.

projects.record: Keep a jar diary: the date, where you see drops, what the plants look like, and a drawing. Write the jar's water cycle with arrows.
projects.context: This is a two-week project. You build a closed jar garden. Its water goes round and round inside, like a tiny Earth, so you never need to water it again.

flow.do: 1. Put the pebbles in the bottom of the jar. 2. Sprinkle the crushed charcoal on top. 3. Add the soil. 4. Make small holes and plant the moss, fern or cutting. Press the soil down gently. 5. Spray or spoon in water until the soil is damp, but no puddle forms at the bottom.
flow.say: We're building a tiny world. The pebbles at the bottom hold extra water away from the roots. The plants will drink from the soil. And once we close the lid, no water can get in or out.
flow.kid: Put pebbles in the jar. Then charcoal. Then soil. Plant your little plants. Add water until the soil is damp, not muddy.
flow.parent: Too much water is the most common mistake. The soil should feel like a squeezed-out sponge. Moss from a shady wall and a money plant cutting usually do well. Avoid cactus and plants that need full sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Rain Forest in a Jar. You build a small garden inside a glass jar.

flow.do: Close the lid and put the jar near a bright window, but out of direct sunshine.
flow.say: Now we close it. From today, no new water goes in. Will the plants survive?
flow.kid: Close the lid. Put it near a bright window, not in the hot sun. No more watering!
flow.wait: Check the jar tomorrow, in the morning and in the afternoon.

flow.do: On days 2, 4 and 7, look closely at the jar. Draw where the drops are. Notice if they are on the walls, the lid or the leaves.
flow.say: Where is the water now? Is it in the soil, the plants, the air or on the glass? Is it the same in the morning and the afternoon?
flow.kid: Look at your jar. Where are the drops? Draw them. Is it different in the morning and the afternoon?
flow.parent: Drops usually appear on the glass in the morning. They may clear later, as the jar warms. Is the glass always fogged and the soil soggy? Then open the lid for a few hours to let some water out. If you see white fuzzy mould, take out that leaf, and open the lid for a day.

check.q: In the closed jar garden, drops form on the inside of the glass. Where did they come from?
options: Water evaporated from the soil and leaves, and condensed on the cooler glass
Water leaked in through the lid
The glass made them
check.why: The lid is closed, so no water can get in. Water evaporates from the damp soil, and leaves give off vapour. When the vapour touches the cooler glass, it condenses into drops. The drops run down into the soil, and the cycle starts again.

flow.do: On day 14, compare the jar with your day 1 drawing. Then your child explains the jar's water cycle to someone else in the family.
flow.say: Two weeks, and we never watered it. In England, a man called David Latimer planted a bottle garden in 1960. He watered it only once more, in 1972. It was still growing more than 50 years later. Tell someone how our jar keeps its plants alive.
flow.kid: Two weeks with no watering! Tell someone how the water in your jar goes round. Use the words evaporate and condense.
flow.think: The Earth is a bit like a closed jar in space. What would happen if someone took the lid off?

challenges.title: Beat the Sun: keep the water from evaporating
challenges.problem: On a hot day, ponds, tanks and reservoirs lose lots of water to evaporation. Your job: leave 10 spoons of water in the sun for a whole day, and have as much left as possible at the end.
constraints: Every container starts with exactly 10 teaspoons of water.
It must stay in the same sunny place as an open bowl, the 'control', for the whole day.
You can only use things you find at home.
At the end, count the spoons left using the same spoon.
materials: 3 or 4 small steel bowls or katoris of the same size
things from home: a lid, a plate, cling film, a cloth, leaves, a few drops of cooking oil, a narrow bottle
general: Cover the water with a lid or cling film, so the vapour can't escape.
Put it in a deep, narrow container, so less water is at the top.
Shade it with a plate, a cloth or leaves.
creative: Float a few drops of cooking oil on top. A thin layer of oil slows evaporation. Scientists have tested floating layers like this on reservoirs.
In Gujarat, solar panels have been put on top of canals since 2012. They make electricity and shade the water, so less of it evaporates.
Old stepwells keep water deep down, in cool shade, far below the hot air. Could you make a tiny stepwell?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to beat the Sun. Draw it, build it, and test it against the open bowl for a whole day. How many spoons did you save?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You must stop water from evaporating in the hot sun, using what you know about what makes evaporation fast.

flow.do: 1. Put 10 teaspoons of water in each bowl. 2. One bowl stays open. It is the control, the bowl you compare with.
flow.say: This open bowl shows what the Sun does if we don't stop it. Your ideas have to beat it.
flow.kid: Put 10 spoons of water in each bowl. One bowl stays open. Your ideas must beat it!
flow.context: This is the first step of Beat the Sun. You set up an open bowl of water to compare your ideas against.

flow.do: List three ideas before building anything. Think about what made water evaporate fastest in the Evaporation Race.
flow.say: Remember the race. Sun, wind and a wide surface all made water go faster. How can we block each one?
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas first. What made water dry fastest in the race? Block it!

flow.do: 1. Build your three ideas. 2. Put them all in the same sunny spot as the open bowl, in the morning. 3. Leave them all day.
flow.say: They must all sit in the same sun, for the same time, so the test is fair.
flow.kid: Build your ideas. Put them all in the sun with the open bowl. Leave them all day.
flow.wait: Leave the bowls in the sun until evening.

flow.do: In the evening, count the spoons left in each bowl, using the same spoon. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: Let's count. How many spoons did the open bowl lose? Which idea saved the most?
flow.kid: Count the spoons left in each bowl. Which idea saved the most water?
flow.parent: On a hot, sunny day, the open bowl often loses half its water or more. A covered bowl usually loses almost none, though drops form under the lid. If it is cool or cloudy, leave them a second day. If you used oil, do not pour that water on plants. Wipe the bowl with soap.

check.q: In Beat the Sun, a bowl covered with cling film kept almost all its water. Why?
options: The vapour condensed on the film and dripped back, instead of escaping into the air
The film kept the Sun's heat out completely
Water cannot evaporate under plastic
check.why: Water still evaporated under the film. You could see drops on it. But the vapour could not escape. It condensed on the film and dripped back down. Picking 'kept the heat out' is a natural guess, but clear film lets sunlight through.

flow.think: Big reservoirs lose a lot of water to evaporation. Should we cover them? What might go wrong?

setup.caption: 1. Put 10 spoons of water in each bowl. Leave one open.

setup.caption: 2. Draw three ideas before you build.

challenges.title: The Fog Catcher: water for a dry hill
challenges.problem: Some dry places, high in the hills by the sea, get almost no rain, but thick fog drifts past most mornings. Design a net that catches water from the fog and drips it into a pot.
constraints: It must be cheap, light and easy to build.
It must stand up on its own, or hang from something.
It must lead the drops into one container.
Test it with 'fog' from a spray bottle in front of a fan.
materials: a spray bottle that makes a fine mist
things to make a net: an old onion or fruit net bag, an old mosquito net, a tea strainer, a piece of cloth, a comb, string
a tray or a bowl to catch the drips
general: Hang a fine net upright, facing the fog, like a volleyball net.
Put a gutter or a tray along the bottom to catch the drips.
Use a net with many fine threads, so lots of tiny drops hit it.
creative: In Chile, in the dry Atacama desert, villages have used big fog-catching nets since the 1980s.
In Morocco, a group called Dar Si Hmad set up fog nets in 2015 to bring water to mountain villages.
A beetle in the Namib desert tilts its back into the morning fog. Drops gather on its back and roll down to its mouth.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own fog catcher. Draw it, build it and test it. How many drops can you catch in 3 minutes of 'fog'?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge about condensation and catching water. You design a net that collects drops from fog, like villages in dry mountains do.

flow.do: 1. Set the fan on low, pointing at a wall or a window. 2. Spray mist from the bottle in front of the fan, so it blows like fog. 3. Feel the 'fog' on your hand.
flow.say: Fog is a cloud on the ground, billions of tiny drops. Feel it on your hand. Your job is to catch it.
flow.kid: Turn the fan on low. Spray mist in front of it. That is your fog! Feel it on your hand.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Fog Catcher. You make 'fog' with a spray bottle and a fan.

flow.do: Draw three designs before building anything.
flow.say: Think about this. Tiny fog drops pass through big holes. What kind of net will catch them?
flow.kid: Draw three fog catchers. Think: what will tiny drops bump into?

flow.do: 1. Build each design. 2. Stand it in the fog, with a tray underneath. 3. Spray 30 times in front of the fan. 4. Count the drops in the tray, or measure them with a spoon.
flow.say: Test each catcher with exactly the same fog: 30 sprays each. Which one catches the most?
flow.kid: Test each catcher with 30 sprays. Count the drops in the tray. Which one wins?
flow.parent: A fine onion net or mosquito net usually works best. Drops gather on the threads, join into bigger drops and run down. A solid cloth gets wet but drips less. Wipe up the floor afterwards, so nobody slips.

check.q: In the Fog Catcher challenge, why does a net with fine threads catch more water than a net with big holes?
options: More tiny drops bump into the threads, stick and join into bigger drops
Fine threads are colder
Big holes make the fog go faster
check.why: Fog drops are tiny and float past most things. Fine threads give them many more chances to bump in and stick. When many tiny drops join, they become heavy enough to run down. That is like cloud drops joining to make rain.

flow.do: Compare your design with the usual solutions and the creative ideas.
flow.say: A beetle in the Namib desert solved this long ago. Which idea would you copy for a real village?
flow.kid: A desert beetle drinks fog that gathers on its back! Which idea would you use for a real village?
flow.think: Nature had millions of years to find water in dry places. What else could we learn from desert plants and animals?

opts: Water going round and round between the sea, the air and the land
Rain falling once and then stopping
quiz.why: Water rises, falls and flows back, again and again. Picking 'falling once' sees only one step. Almost no new water is made. The same water keeps going round.

quiz.p: A puddle dries up on a sunny day. What happened to its water?
opts: It evaporated into the air as invisible vapour
It was destroyed by the Sun
It all soaked into the cement
quiz.why: The water went into the air. Water is never destroyed by drying. Picking 'soaked in' can be partly true on soil, but cement has almost no holes.

quiz.p: A cold tumbler of ice gets wet on the outside. What is this called?
quiz.why: Vapour from the air cools on the cold steel and turns into drops. That is condensation. Picking 'melting' means thinking the ice got through the steel. The drops are not salty or coloured like the water inside, so they came from the air.

opts: Tiny drops of water or ice crystals
quiz.why: Clouds are made of tiny drops or ice. You can see them, and vapour is invisible. Picking 'vapour' is the most common mistake, even in some books.

quiz.p: In the Cloud in a Jar, what did the smoke do?
opts: It gave the vapour tiny specks to condense on
quiz.why: Vapour needs specks to make drops. Smoke, dust and sea salt are the seeds of real cloud drops. Picking 'turned into rain' mixes up the seeds with the water.

quiz.p: Why is rain fresh, when the sea is salty?
opts: Only water evaporates. The salt stays behind.
Rain comes from rivers, not the sea
quiz.why: Salt cannot evaporate at everyday temperatures, so only fresh water rises. Picking 'filter' means imagining the cloud as a sieve. Picking 'rivers' forgets that most rain rose from the sea.

quiz.p: In Sea in a Bowl, the water in the cup tasted…
opts: Exactly as salty as the bowl
quiz.why: Only water rose and condensed on the cling film. The salt stayed in the bowl. If it tasted salty, some bowl water splashed into the cup.

quiz.p: Look at the Evaporation Race results. Which made water dry fastest?
opts: The narrow glass in the shade
quiz.why: The sunny plate's bar is shortest, 40 minutes. A short bar here means a quick dry. Picking the glass means reading the tallest bar as the winner.

quiz.p: In the Evaporation Race, to make the test fair, what must be the same for every plate?
quiz.why: Every puddle started with exactly 2 teaspoons. Only the place changed. Picking 'the place' gets it backwards: the place is the one thing we change on purpose.

quiz.p: A clear bag tied over a leafy branch fills with mist. Where does the water come from?
opts: From the leaves: plants give off water
quiz.why: Water comes up from the roots and leaves through tiny holes in the leaves. That is transpiration. The empty bag next to it stayed dry, which shows the water came from the leaves.

quiz.p: Why does Mumbai get much more rain than Pune?
opts: Wet winds drop their rain on the Western Ghats before reaching Pune
quiz.why: Wet sea air rises up the mountains, cools and rains on the sea side. The far side is a rain shadow. Distance from the Sun makes no difference here.

quiz.p: When does the monsoon usually reach Kerala?
quiz.why: The monsoon usually arrives in Kerala around the first of June, and covers all of India by about 8 July. October is when it is usually leaving.

quiz.p: Where does the energy to lift water into the sky come from?
quiz.why: The Sun warms water so its molecules break free and rise. That energy comes out again when vapour condenses in clouds. Wind helps carry vapour, but the energy to evaporate it comes from the Sun.

quiz.p: Do scientists fully know how tiny cloud drops grow into raindrops so fast in warm clouds?
opts: No, they are still studying it
Yes, the Moon pulls them together
quiz.why: Scientists know drops bump and join, and that ice helps in cold clouds. But in warm monsoon clouds, rain often forms faster than expected. Swirling air may be part of the answer. It is still being studied.

quiz.p: On Titan, Saturn's biggest moon, it rains…
quiz.why: Titan is so cold that water is rock-hard ice. Methane is liquid there, and it rains, makes rivers and fills lakes. So a 'water cycle' can happen with other liquids too.

applications: Salt pans in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu make salt by letting sea water evaporate in the sun.
Solar stills make drinking water from salty or dirty water in dry places and on lifeboats.
Desalination works near Chennai remove the salt from sea water to make drinking water for the city.
Weather satellites, such as India's INSAT satellites, photograph clouds to forecast rain and cyclones.
India's weather office, the IMD, tracks where the monsoon has reached and advises farmers when to sow.
Pressure cookers and steamers cook food with water vapour.
Clothes dryers and drying racks on terraces use sun, heat and wind to speed up evaporation.
Air conditioners and dehumidifiers take water out of the air by condensation. That is why an AC drips outside.
Fog nets catch drinking water from fog in dry mountains, in Chile and Morocco.
Cloud seeding tries to make suitable clouds give a little more rain.
Cooling towers at power stations cool water by evaporation.
Distilled water for car batteries, hospitals and laboratories is made by boiling water and condensing the steam.
Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh makes a perfume called mitti attar, which smells of first rain, by heating baked clay and condensing the vapour.
Solar panels on top of canals in Gujarat make electricity and cut evaporation.
Sealed jar gardens and greenhouses recycle their own water.
