open_questions.q: How do tiny cloud drops grow into raindrops so fast in warm clouds?
open_questions.why_open: Rain often forms faster than older ideas predict. Swirling air may throw drops together, but it happens inside clouds, at a tiny scale, and is very hard to measure.

open_questions.q: How will the Indian monsoon change as the world warms?
open_questions.why_open: Heavy rain days are already more common in central India. But the monsoon depends on the oceans, the land and the winds together, and forecasts for 50 years ahead still disagree.

open_questions.q: How much does cloud seeding really work?
open_questions.why_open: It is hard to know how much a cloud would have rained anyway. Tests in India and elsewhere find small effects, only in suitable clouds.

open_questions.q: Do forests pull rain inland from the sea, or only recycle it?
open_questions.why_open: Forests clearly recycle rain. Whether they also pull in wet air from the sea, as the 'biotic pump' idea says, is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How much do tiny living things in clouds help make rain and snow?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria that make ice have been found in snow from many countries. Nobody yet knows how much they change the world's rain.

open_questions.q: Why are clouds the hardest part of predicting future climate?
open_questions.why_open: Clouds both cool the Earth, by blocking sunlight, and warm it, by trapping heat. Which wins depends on the kind of cloud, its height and the place. Computers struggle with them, because clouds are small and change fast.

open_questions.q: Could there be other worlds with water cycles like ours?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found many planets around other stars. A few might have seas and clouds, but our telescopes can only just begin to check.

maths.problem: In the Evaporation Race, the sunny plate dried in 40 minutes and the shady plate took 120 minutes. How many times as long did the shady plate take?
maths.explain: The shady plate took 120 minutes. The sunny plate took 40 minutes. 120 divided by 40 is 3. You can check: 40 + 40 + 40 = 120. So in the shade, the water took 3 times as long to evaporate.
maths.context: This is about the Evaporation Race. You put 2 teaspoons of water in four places and timed how long each took to dry.

maths.problem: Your solar still collects about 5 millilitres of fresh water every hour. How much does it collect in 4 hours? A person needs about 2 litres, which is 2,000 millilitres, to drink in a day. How many stills like yours would one person need for one day of 4 sunny hours?
maths.answer: 20 millilitres in 4 hours. One person would need 100 stills.
maths.explain: Each hour gives 5 millilitres. 4 hours give 4 × 5 = 20 millilitres. One person needs 2,000 millilitres. 2,000 divided by 20 is 100. So one person would need 100 bowls like yours. That is why real solar stills are big, and why fresh water is precious.
maths.context: This is about Sea in a Bowl. You made fresh water from salty water with a bowl, a cup, cling film and sunshine.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small amount by the hours, then comparing it with what a person needs, shows how much sunshine it takes to make drinking water.

maths.problem: Look at the measuring spoon picture. In the leaf-in-a-bag experiment, you poured the water from the bag into a 5 millilitre teaspoon. It filled the spoon halfway. How many millilitres did the branch give off?
maths.explain: A full teaspoon holds 5 millilitres. Half of 5 is 2 and a half. So the branch gave off about 2 and a half millilitres in 3 hours. A big tree has thousands of branches, so it can give off many litres in a day.
maths.context: This is about Leaves in a Bag. You tied a clear bag over a leafy branch for 3 hours, and collected the water that came out of the leaves.
maths.why_maths: Measuring with halves of a spoon turns 'a few drops' into a real number, so we can compare one branch with a whole tree.

maths.problem: Mumbai gets about 2,200 millimetres of rain in a year. Pune gets about 700 millimetres. Draw a bar chart of the two cities. How much more rain does Mumbai get?
maths.answer: Mumbai gets about 1,500 millimetres more rain than Pune. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each city. Mumbai's bar goes up to 2,200 and Pune's to 700. To find the difference, take away: 2,200 − 700 = 1,500. So Mumbai gets about 1,500 millimetres more. That is one and a half metres more rain in a year.
maths.context: This is about Make a Monsoon. You traced the monsoon on a map and found Mumbai, on the sea side of the Western Ghats, and Pune, just beyond them.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows the rain shadow at a glance: one tall bar on the sea side of the mountains and a short one beyond.

maths.problem: On average, water stays in the air for about 9 days before it falls. Let's round that to 10 days. About how many times could the same water go up into the air and come down again in one year of 360 days?
maths.explain: Each trip takes about 10 days. In 360 days, there are 360 ÷ 10 = 36 lots of 10 days. So, if it kept going straight back up, it could make about 36 trips. Real water often waits in a river, the ground or the sea in between, so most water makes far fewer.
maths.context: This is about How Long Does a Drop Stay? You pegged cards on a line to show how long water stays in each part of the water cycle.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a year by the length of one trip shows how fast the air part of the water cycle really is.

maths.problem: After playing Round the World Drop, a child counted the beads on their bracelet: 4 blue (sea), 3 white (cloud), 2 green (river) and 1 light green (plant). Make a tally chart and a bar chart. Which place did the drop visit most?
maths.answer: The sea, with 4 beads. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Count each colour and make a tally: sea 4, cloud 3, river 2, plant 1. Then draw one bar for each place. The sea's bar is the tallest, at 4. That fits the real world, because most of Earth's water is in the sea. 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 beads, one for each turn.
maths.context: This is about Round the World Drop, the bead bracelet game. You collected one bead for each place your drop visited.
maths.why_maths: Turning a bracelet of beads into a tally and a chart shows where water spends most of its time.

roots.context: We have been learning how water goes up into the air, turns into clouds and comes down as rain. Now we ask what the water cycle tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The air in a room that looks empty holds water you cannot see. Cool that air, and drops appear on a cold plate. A cloud forms the same way, from water already in the clear sky. So clear air is not empty: our eyes simply cannot see water as a gas.
deep_truth.habit: We call air that looks clear 'empty', and we think a cloud is water arriving in the sky. But water vapour is invisible, so our eyes cannot tell us whether water is there.
deep_truth.evidence: In A Cloud in a Jar, a cloud appeared in clear air as soon as the icy plate cooled it. Your breath misted a cold plate, then vanished into the air again. In The Cold Tumbler, clear, plain drops came out of the room's air.

three.who_am_i: More than half of your body is water. Every breath you breathe out carries some of it into the air, where nobody can see it.
three.what_is_life: Life is part of the water cycle. Plants lift water from the soil and give it to the air. Animals drink the rain and give it back.
three.what_is_this_world: In this world, sea water rises into the sky and comes back down as rain and rivers, again and again. Much of this journey happens where we cannot see it.

roots.thread: The same water is sea, then invisible vapour, then a cloud, rain, a river and part of a neem tree. We give each of these a different name, but it is one water changing form. The whole world is like this: one source taking many forms, some seen and some unseen. The water cycle is a place where you can watch one water become many things, and come back again.

teachings.teaching: The Upanishad describes a journey. One becomes air, then smoke, then mist, then a cloud. The cloud rains down, and one is born again as rice, barley, plants and trees.
teachings.link: The Upanishad is about what happens to a person after death, not about weather. But it pictures life travelling with water: from the sky, as rain, into plants. That is the path the water cycle really takes.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker, about 2,500 years ago (Fragment 12, as numbered by the scholars Diels and Kranz)
teachings.teaching: As people step into the same rivers, different waters keep flowing past them.
teachings.link: A river keeps its name, but its water is always new. A cloud is the same: its drops keep drying up at the edges while new ones form.

teachings.teaching: All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full. The rivers go back to the place they came from, and flow again.
teachings.link: The writer had noticed the puzzle: rivers pour into the sea for ever, but it never overflows. The water cycle is the answer.

science.text: On average, a water molecule stays in the air for only about 9 days before it falls again. The water in a cloud is always new.
The water in your body is replaced again and again. Studies that trace water with special labels show that an adult swaps a few litres of body water every day, out of about 40 litres.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: The Charvakas said that only what we can perceive with our senses is real. For them the world is just earth, water, fire and air mixing, with no one source behind it. The water cycle, they would say, is simply water and heat doing what they do, and nothing more needs to be added. It is an honest view, and many careful people hold something like it today.

practice.title: Make a cloud with your breath
practice.say: Hold a steel plate or a mirror close to your mouth. Breathe out slowly onto it with an open mouth, like a sigh. Watch the mist appear. Now stay still and watch it shrink, from the edges in, until it is gone. That mist was inside you a moment ago. Now it is in the air of this room. You cannot see it, but it is still there. Breathe again. Watch it come, and watch it go. Where does your breath end and the air begin?
practice.kid: Hold a steel plate near your mouth. Breathe out slowly, like a sigh. See the mist? Watch it vanish. It was inside you. Now it is in the air, still there but invisible.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home today. Sea in a Bowl needs a hot, sunny day: drops show within 30 minutes, but a full cup takes 3 to 4 hours and gives only a spoonful or two. A cloudy-day version with ice and a pan of hot water is given. The Cloud in a Jar is the quickest and most reliable result, which is why it is in the spine: with agarbatti smoke, a dark cloth and a torch, a thick cloud forms in about 30 seconds. Without smoke it is only a thin mist, so the comparison works. Dew does not form on hot, dry summer nights, so the Dew Walk offers an ice tumbler instead. The leaf bag works best on a big leafy bush in sun. A small pot plant may give only drops. In Round the World Drop, the DEW card was unreachable in the first draft, so the PLANT card now sends drops there on a 1, and a solo rule was added: play two bracelets and compare. The molecule game needs at least two people, so it is marked for a parent or friends only. Timings were checked: the experiments that need hours of sun count only the minutes a family is busy, with the waiting shown as a wait step. Parents should know: a grown-up handles hot water, steam, matches and agarbatti, and children taste only the fresh water from the cup, never the salty bowl. Rewrite check: the Evaporation Race glass is now shown as still wet at 3 hours, because 2 teaspoons in a narrow glass in the shade usually takes many hours. Sea in a Bowl uses all of its 2 cups of salty water, which makes a shallow layer in a big bowl. A cut-open clear plastic bag can replace cling film.

how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, many learned people in Europe believed rain was far too little to keep rivers flowing all year. They thought sea water travelled through hidden passages under the mountains and came out as springs. In 1580, Bernard Palissy, a French potter who had never been to university, wrote that springs and rivers come only from rain soaking into the ground. Few scholars listened, because he had no measurements. About ninety years later, Pierre Perrault measured the rain falling on the land around the start of the river Seine for three years. He also worked out how much water the river carried. In 1674, he showed that the rain was about six times more than the river carried. Soon after, Edmond Halley measured how fast water evaporates from a warmed pan. He worked out that the Sun lifts enough water from the sea to make all the rain. Careful measuring, not arguing, settled the question.
how_we_found_out.who: Bernard Palissy, Pierre Perrault and Edmond Halley
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Rivers and springs are fed by sea water rising through hidden passages under the mountains, because rain is far too little.
